title: Pressure injury prevention nursing care plan
summary: Structured nursing care plan to prevent pressure injuries in at-risk inpatients, using validated risk assessment (e.g. Braden Scale), skin inspection, repositioning, support surfaces, nutrition and moisture management.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Perform a structured pressure-injury risk assessment within 6 hours of admission using a validated tool (e.g. Braden Scale assessing sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, friction/shear).
Inspect skin (especially bony prominences: sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities, occiput) at least daily and on every position change.
Identify reversible risk factors: immobility, incontinence, poor nutrition/hydration, reduced perfusion, altered sensation.

steps.detail: Reposition at-risk patients on a documented schedule, repositioning frequency individualised to the person, their skin and the support surface; offload heels.
Provide a pressure-redistributing mattress/cushion for at-risk patients rather than a standard mattress.
Keep skin clean and dry; use barrier products; manage incontinence promptly to limit moisture-associated skin damage.
Refer high-risk or malnourished patients for nutritional assessment and support adequate protein, energy and fluid intake.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Reassess risk after any change in condition and document skin status each shift.
Record repositioning and skin checks; escalate if new non-blanchable erythema (Category/Stage 1) appears.
Evaluate care plan effectiveness and update interventions as risk changes.

redFlags: New non-blanchable erythema, blister, or open lesion over a bony prominence — assess, stage and escalate.
Signs of infection in an existing pressure injury (spreading erythema, purulence, systemic sepsis).

references.label: NICE CG179 — Pressure ulcers: prevention and management
EPUAP/NPIAP/PPPIA International Clinical Practice Guideline — Prevention and Treatment of Pressure Ulcers/Injuries

title: Pressure ulcer staging and management
summary: Classification of pressure injuries by category/stage (NPUAP/EPUAP system) and corresponding nursing management, including wound assessment, dressing selection and escalation.

sections.heading: Staging (NPUAP/EPUAP category/stage)
items: Category/Stage 1: intact skin with non-blanchable erythema (colour change in darker skin tones).
Category/Stage 2: partial-thickness skin loss — shallow open ulcer or intact/ruptured blister; no slough.
Category/Stage 3: full-thickness skin loss; subcutaneous fat may be visible; bone/tendon/muscle not exposed.
Category/Stage 4: full-thickness tissue loss with exposed bone, tendon or muscle.
Unstageable: full-thickness loss where the base is obscured by slough/eschar.
Suspected deep tissue injury: localised purple/maroon discolouration or blood-filled blister.

steps.detail: Record category/stage, size, exudate, tissue type, surrounding skin and pain at each dressing change.
Reposition and use pressure-redistributing surfaces; never position the patient directly on the ulcer.
Choose a dressing matched to wound bed and exudate (e.g. moisture-retentive dressings); promote moist wound healing.
Treat clinical infection and refer for debridement of devitalised tissue per local policy.

redFlags: Spreading cellulitis, systemic sepsis, or rapidly deteriorating wound.
Exposed bone with suspected osteomyelitis.

references.label: NICE CG179 — Pressure ulcers: prevention and management
NPUAP Revised Pressure Injury Staging System (2016)

title: Inpatient falls prevention nursing care plan
summary: Multifactorial falls risk assessment and individualised intervention plan for hospitalised adults, with emphasis on older inpatients.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Consider all patients aged 65 and over, and those 50–64 with underlying conditions, at risk; perform a multifactorial falls risk assessment.
Assess: falls history, gait/balance and mobility, cognition/delirium, continence, medication (especially sedatives, antihypertensives), vision, footwear, postural blood pressure.
Identify environmental hazards at the bedside.

steps.detail: Review and rationalise culprit medications, manage postural hypotension, optimise vision and continence.
Ensure call bell within reach, bed at safe height, clear walkways, non-slip footwear and adequate lighting.
Provide appropriate walking aids and supervised mobilisation; involve physiotherapy.
Flag high-risk patients, educate patient and family, and consider increased observation.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Reassess after any fall or change in condition and document a post-fall review.
Evaluate effectiveness of interventions and update the plan.

redFlags: Fall with head injury on anticoagulants — urgent imaging.
Fall with suspected fracture, loss of consciousness, or new neurological deficit.

references.label: NICE CG161 — Falls in older people: assessing risk and prevention

title: Acute pain management nursing care plan
summary: Nursing care plan for assessment and management of acute pain in hospitalised adults using regular validated pain assessment and a stepwise analgesic approach.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Assess pain regularly using a validated tool (e.g. numeric rating scale, or a behavioural tool for non-verbal patients).
Characterise pain: site, onset, character, radiation, severity, timing, exacerbating/relieving factors.
Assess impact on function, sleep and mood; screen for neuropathic features.

steps.detail: Use regular non-opioid analgesia (e.g. paracetamol) as a base, adding opioids for moderate-to-severe pain titrated to response, following the prescription and local protocol.
Positioning, splinting, heat/cold, reassurance and distraction as appropriate.
With opioids, monitor sedation and respiratory rate, and provide laxatives and antiemetics as needed.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Reassess pain after each intervention to evaluate effectiveness.
Monitor for opioid toxicity (sedation, respiratory depression) and adjust the plan.

redFlags: Sudden severe pain or pain disproportionate to findings (consider ischaemia, compartment syndrome).
Respiratory rate falling or increasing sedation after opioids — risk of opioid toxicity.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the pharmacological and radiotherapeutic management of cancer pain (analgesic ladder principles)
NICE — Medicines optimisation in chronic/acute pain (CKS)

title: Peripheral IV cannula care nursing care plan
summary: Care and maintenance of peripheral intravenous cannulae to prevent phlebitis, infiltration and catheter-related infection.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Inspect the cannula site at least once per shift using a structured tool (e.g. Visual Infusion Phlebitis score) for pain, erythema, swelling, palpable cord or leakage.
Check the dressing is intact, dry and the insertion date is documented.
Review daily whether the cannula is still required.

steps.detail: Perform hand hygiene and decontaminate the needle-free connector before each access ('scrub the hub').
Use a sterile transparent semi-permeable dressing allowing site inspection; replace if loose or soiled.
Flush before and after use per local policy to maintain patency.
Remove the cannula as soon as it is no longer needed, or immediately if phlebitis/infiltration occurs.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Document site checks and any complications.
Escalate signs of infection or thrombophlebitis.

redFlags: Spreading erythema, pus, or systemic signs of infection at/around the site.
Severe pain, swelling or limb compromise suggesting infiltration/extravasation of a vesicant.

references.label: RCN Standards for infusion therapy
epic3 / NICE CG139 — Healthcare-associated infections: prevention and control (intravascular devices)

title: Indwelling urinary catheter care nursing care plan
summary: Nursing care of patients with an indwelling urinary catheter to maintain drainage, comfort and prevent catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI).

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Review daily whether the catheter is still clinically indicated and document the rationale and insertion date.
Assess urine output, colour and clarity; assess for blockage, bypassing or discomfort.
Assess for signs of CAUTI.

steps.detail: Keep the drainage system closed and the bag below bladder level; avoid unnecessary disconnection.
Provide routine daily meatal hygiene with soap and water; avoid antiseptics.
Perform hand hygiene, use a clean container, and avoid contaminating the outlet tap.
Remove the catheter as soon as it is no longer required.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Monitor for CAUTI and obstruction; escalate as needed.
Document catheter care and continence outcomes after removal.

redFlags: Fever, rigors, suprapubic/loin pain, new confusion or sepsis in a catheterised patient — consider CAUTI/urosepsis.
Anuria/no drainage with a palpable bladder — suspect blockage; assess and unblock or replace.

references.label: NICE CG139 / epic3 — Prevention of catheter-associated UTI
NICE QS61 — Infection prevention and control: urinary catheters

title: Central venous catheter care nursing care plan
summary: Maintenance care of central venous catheters to preserve function and prevent central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI).

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Review daily whether the central line is still required and remove non-essential lines promptly.
Inspect the exit site for erythema, tenderness, swelling or discharge at each dressing change.
Check dressing integrity and that the line is secured.

steps.detail: Perform hand hygiene and use aseptic technique for all line access and dressing changes.
Disinfect needle-free connectors/hubs before every access ('scrub the hub').

Use a chlorhexidine-based skin antiseptic and a sterile transparent dressing; change gauze dressings approximately every 48 hours and transparent dressings up to every 7 days (or sooner if soiled/loose) per local policy.
Flush/lock lumens according to local policy to maintain patency.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Document daily line review and site assessment.
Escalate suspected CLABSI per local pathway.

redFlags: Fever/rigors, especially on line flushing, with no other source — suspect CLABSI; take cultures and escalate.
Exit-site purulence or spreading erythema.

references.label: CDC Guidelines for the Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections
epic3 / NICE CG139 — central venous access devices

title: Wound assessment and dressing selection care plan
summary: Structured wound assessment and principles of dressing selection to support moist wound healing and manage exudate and infection.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Assess wound type, size, depth, wound bed tissue (granulation, slough, eschar), exudate level, odour and surrounding skin.
Assess for clinical signs of infection and underlying cause (pressure, venous, arterial, diabetic, surgical, traumatic).
Assess pain and patient factors affecting healing (nutrition, perfusion, glycaemic control).

steps.step: Match dressing to the wound bed
steps.detail: Promote a moist wound-healing environment; choose dressings appropriate to tissue type and exudate volume.
Use absorbent dressings for high exudate and hydrating dressings for dry wounds to protect peri-wound skin.
Consider antimicrobial dressings for localised infection and treat spreading/systemic infection per policy.
Use barrier products and atraumatic dressings to minimise maceration and skin stripping.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Reassess at each dressing change and document progress; reduce dressing frequency as the wound improves.
Escalate non-healing or deteriorating wounds for specialist review.

redFlags: Spreading cellulitis, systemic sepsis, or rapidly enlarging wound.
Exposed bone/tendon, deep tracking, or suspected necrotising infection (severe pain, crepitus, rapid spread).

references.label: NICE — Chronic wounds: advanced wound dressings and antimicrobial dressings (ESMPB2)

title: Post-operative nursing care plan
summary: Immediate and ongoing post-operative nursing care covering airway, breathing, circulation, pain, wound, fluid balance and early recognition of complications.

sections.heading: Immediate recovery assessment
items: Assess airway patency, breathing and oxygenation; provide oxygen as prescribed.
Monitor vital signs using a track-and-trigger early warning score and escalate per protocol.
Assess level of consciousness, pain, nausea, surgical site/drains and fluid balance.

steps.detail: Provide prescribed analgesia and antiemetics; reassess effectiveness.
Observe the wound for bleeding/haematoma and record drain output; maintain dressings.
Monitor intake/output and IV fluids; watch for signs of hypovolaemia or overload.
Encourage early mobilisation, deep breathing, VTE prophylaxis as prescribed, and pressure-injury prevention.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Continue observation frequency guided by early warning score and recovery.
Document recovery milestones and escalate deterioration.

redFlags: Rising early warning score: tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxia, tachypnoea, reduced consciousness — escalate urgently.
Brisk wound bleeding, expanding haematoma, or signs of post-operative haemorrhage.
Acute severe pain, new breathlessness or chest pain (consider PE).

references.label: NICE NG180 — Perioperative care in adults
RCN — Post-anaesthetic recovery guidance

title: Oxygen therapy nursing care plan
summary: Safe administration and monitoring of oxygen therapy, prescribing to a target saturation range and avoiding both hypoxaemia and hyperoxaemia.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Confirm oxygen is prescribed with a target saturation range; typical target is 94–98% for most acutely unwell adults, and 88–92% for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (e.g. COPD).
Assess work of breathing, respiratory rate and SpO2; obtain ABG where hypercapnia is a concern.
Confirm correct delivery device for the required flow/FiO2.

steps.detail: Adjust the delivery device and flow to keep SpO2 within the prescribed target range; wean as the patient improves.
Use nasal cannulae for low-flow needs, simple/Venturi masks or reservoir masks for higher requirements, per the target.
Secure tubing, check humidification if needed, and observe fire-safety precautions (no smoking/naked flames).

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Monitor SpO2 continuously or at set intervals and document FiO2/flow.
Reassess after changes; escalate if oxygen requirement rises or saturation falls below target.

redFlags: Falling SpO2 despite increasing oxygen — escalate urgently.
In COPD/at-risk patients: rising drowsiness/confusion with high-flow oxygen — suspect hypercapnia, check ABG.

references.label: BTS Guideline for oxygen use in adults in healthcare and emergency settings

title: Nasogastric tube care nursing care plan
summary: Ongoing nursing care of a nasogastric (NG) feeding tube, including position confirmation before use to prevent misplacement and aspiration.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Confirm tube position before first use, before each feed/medication, and after vomiting, coughing or signs of displacement.
Aspirate gastric contents and test with pH indicator paper: a pH of 5.5 or below is the first-line indicator of gastric placement.
Check the documented external tube length against the recorded insertion length.

steps.detail: Feed only when aspirate pH is 5.5 or below; if pH is above 5.5 or no aspirate is obtained, do not use the tube and follow local protocol (repositioning, waiting, or chest X-ray).
Chest X-ray is the second-line check when aspirate cannot be obtained or pH is unreliable; interpretation must be by a competent practitioner.
Flush before and after feeds/medications, secure the tube, and provide nasal and oral care.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Document position checks and tube length each shift.
Monitor for aspiration, displacement and feed tolerance.

redFlags: NEVER feed via an NG tube whose gastric position is unconfirmed — misplacement into the lung can be fatal (a Never Event).
New respiratory distress, coughing or desaturation during/after feeding — stop and reassess position.

references.label: NHS Improvement / NPSA — Nasogastric tube misplacement: continuing risk of death and severe harm

title: Blood transfusion administration and monitoring care plan
summary: Safe administration and monitoring of blood components, with rigorous identity checks and structured observations to detect acute transfusion reactions early.

sections.heading: Pre-transfusion checks
items: Confirm a valid prescription, consent and patent IV access.
Perform the final bedside identity check at the patient's side: positively identify the patient and match details on the wristband, the component and the compatibility label.
Record baseline temperature, pulse, blood pressure and respiratory rate immediately before starting.

steps.detail: Begin the transfusion and observe the patient closely; most acute reactions occur within the first 15 minutes.
Record temperature, pulse, blood pressure and respiratory rate at 15 minutes after the start of each unit.
Monitor per local policy during the transfusion and on completion; transfuse each unit within the recommended time limit.
STOP the transfusion, maintain IV access with saline, reassess the patient and re-check the identity of the unit against the patient, and call for help.

redFlags: Fever, rigors, hypotension, loin/chest pain, breathlessness or collapse during transfusion — STOP immediately; suspect acute haemolytic (ABO incompatibility) or other severe reaction.
Even a few millilitres of ABO-incompatible blood can cause a life-threatening acute haemolytic reaction.

references.label: British Society for Haematology — Guideline on the administration of blood components
NICE NG24 — Blood transfusion

title: Delirium prevention and care plan
summary: Identification of at-risk patients, multicomponent non-pharmacological prevention, screening and management of delirium in hospital.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Identify patients at risk (age 65+, cognitive impairment/dementia, hip fracture, severe illness).
Screen for delirium using a validated tool (e.g. 4AT) and assess for acute change or fluctuation in cognition, attention and alertness.
Identify and address precipitating factors: infection, pain, dehydration, constipation, hypoxia, urinary retention, medications.

steps.detail: Reorientation, ensuring glasses/hearing aids, promoting sleep hygiene, early mobilisation, hydration and nutrition, and avoiding unnecessary catheters/lines.
Identify and manage precipitants such as infection, pain, hypoxia, electrolyte disturbance and medication effects.
Use verbal de-escalation and involve family; reserve pharmacological management for severe distress or risk, at the lowest effective dose and shortest duration, per guideline.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Reassess cognition and reorientation regularly; document fluctuations.
Review and rationalise medications; evaluate response to interventions.

redFlags: New or fluctuating confusion in an acutely unwell patient — screen for and treat reversible causes (sepsis, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia).
Hypoactive delirium (drowsiness, withdrawal) is easily missed and carries poor prognosis.

references.label: NICE CG103 — Delirium: prevention, diagnosis and management
SIGN 157 — Risk reduction and management of delirium

title: End-of-life comfort care plan (last days of life)
summary: Individualised nursing care for adults in the last days of life, focusing on comfort, symptom control, communication and dignity.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Recognise when a person may be entering the last days of life through multidisciplinary assessment and review.
Assess symptoms regularly: pain, breathlessness, nausea, agitation, respiratory secretions and mouth dryness.
Explore the wishes, preferences and spiritual/cultural needs of the person and those important to them.

steps.detail: Discuss and agree an individualised care plan with the person (where possible) and family; review preferred place of care.
Anticipate and manage pain, breathlessness, nausea, agitation and respiratory secretions with prescribed medications, including anticipatory ('just in case') medicines.
Mouth care, positioning, pressure-area care, continence care and a calm environment; review need for non-essential interventions and monitoring.
Support oral intake as tolerated; make individualised decisions about clinically assisted hydration with the person and family.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Review symptoms and the care plan at least daily and after any change.
Support the family before and after death, including bereavement.

redFlags: Uncontrolled distressing symptoms (pain, breathlessness, agitation) — escalate to specialist palliative care.

references.label: NICE NG31 — Care of dying adults in the last days of life

title: Sepsis recognition and immediate nursing care plan
summary: Early recognition of deterioration due to suspected sepsis and immediate nursing actions to escalate and support time-critical treatment.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Think 'could this be sepsis?' in any patient with signs of infection and use a track-and-trigger early warning score.

Assess for high-risk criteria: altered mental state, respiratory rate ≥ 25, oxygen needed to maintain saturation, heart rate ≥ 131, systolic BP ≤ 90 mmHg, reduced urine output, mottled/non-blanching rash.
Identify the likely source of infection.

steps.detail: Escalate any high-risk criteria to senior clinical review immediately.
Facilitate the prompt initiation of the treatment bundle (oxygen if needed, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, lactate measurement and urine output monitoring) as prescribed.
Increase observation frequency and continuously reassess response.

redFlags: Any high-risk sepsis criterion (e.g. new confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, mottling) — escalate immediately for senior review.
Non-blanching rash, especially with fever — consider meningococcal sepsis, treat as emergency.

references.label: NICE NG51 — Sepsis: recognition, diagnosis and early management

title: Peripheral intravenous cannulation
summary: Insertion of a peripheral IV cannula for fluid or medication administration using aseptic non-touch technique.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm indication and consent; explain the procedure.
Gather equipment: cannula of appropriate gauge, tourniquet, skin antiseptic (e.g. 2% chlorhexidine in alcohol), sterile dressing, flush, sharps bin, gloves.
Perform hand hygiene and select a suitable vein (typically forearm/dorsum of hand), avoiding joints where possible.

steps.detail: Apply the tourniquet proximally, clean the site with antiseptic and allow it to dry fully.
Anchor the vein, insert the cannula bevel-up at a shallow angle until flashback is seen, then advance the cannula over the needle into the vein.
Release the tourniquet, apply pressure over the vein tip, withdraw the needle and dispose of it directly into the sharps bin.
Connect, flush to confirm patency, secure with a sterile transparent dressing and document insertion date/site.

redFlags: Pain, swelling or resistance to flushing — suggests extravasation/infiltration; remove the cannula.
Arterial puncture (bright pulsatile blood) — remove and apply firm pressure.

references.label: RCN Standards for infusion therapy
WHO Best Practices for Injections and Related Procedures Toolkit

title: Venepuncture (blood sampling)
summary: Phlebotomy for venous blood sampling using a safe, aseptic technique and correct order of draw.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm patient identity, request and required tubes; explain and gain consent.
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves; assemble a closed (vacuum) system where available.
Select an appropriate vein after applying the tourniquet, typically in the antecubital fossa.

steps.detail: Disinfect the skin and allow it to dry; do not re-palpate the cleaned site.
Anchor the vein and insert the needle bevel-up; fill tubes following the correct order of draw to avoid additive cross-contamination.
Release the tourniquet before withdrawing the needle; withdraw and immediately activate the safety device, disposing into the sharps bin.
Apply pressure until bleeding stops; mix tubes by gentle inversion and label at the bedside.

redFlags: Do not keep the tourniquet on longer than recommended (avoid prolonged stasis affecting results).
Sudden severe pain or paraesthesia — possible nerve contact; withdraw the needle.

references.label: WHO Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy

title: Urinary catheterisation (female)
summary: Insertion of an indwelling urinary catheter in a female patient using aseptic technique.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm indication and consent; ensure privacy and a chaperone where appropriate.
Gather a sterile catheter pack, appropriate catheter, sterile lubricant, antiseptic cleansing solution, sterile water-filled syringe for the balloon, and drainage bag.
Perform hand hygiene and use aseptic non-touch technique.

steps.detail: Position supine with knees flexed; with the non-dominant hand separate the labia to expose the urethral meatus and clean it per policy.
Apply sterile lubricant; insert the catheter into the urethra (advancing approximately 4–6 cm in adult females) until urine flows.
Advance a little further, then inflate the balloon with sterile water to the volume stated by the manufacturer (commonly 10 mL for an adult catheter) — never inflate before urine is seen.
Connect to a sterile closed drainage system, gently withdraw until resistance is felt, secure the catheter and document.

redFlags: Pain on balloon inflation or no urine drainage — stop; the balloon may be in the urethra.
Frank haematuria or inability to pass the catheter — seek senior/urology advice.

references.label: NICE QS61 — Infection prevention and control: urinary catheters
epic3 / NICE CG139 — urinary catheter insertion

title: Urinary catheterisation (male)
summary: Insertion of an indwelling urinary catheter in a male patient using aseptic technique.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm indication and consent; ensure privacy and a chaperone where appropriate.
Gather a sterile catheter pack, appropriate catheter, sterile anaesthetic lubricant gel, antiseptic cleansing solution, sterile water-filled syringe, and drainage bag.
Perform hand hygiene and use aseptic non-touch technique.

steps.detail: Retract the foreskin (if present), hold the penis upright and clean the glans/meatus per policy.
Instil sterile anaesthetic lubricant into the urethra and wait; insert the catheter, advancing approximately 17–22 cm (to the bifurcation/hilt) until urine flows.
Only after urine is seen, inflate the balloon with sterile water to the manufacturer's stated volume (commonly 10 mL for an adult catheter).
Connect to a closed drainage system, secure the catheter, and reposition the foreskin to prevent paraphimosis; document.

redFlags: Pain on balloon inflation or no urine drainage — stop; do not force.
Resistance at the prostate/stricture, frank haematuria, or failed attempt — seek senior/urology advice.
Always replace a retracted foreskin to prevent paraphimosis.

references.label: NICE QS61 — Infection prevention and control: urinary catheters
epic3 / NICE CG139 — urinary catheter insertion

title: Nasogastric tube insertion
summary: Insertion of a fine-bore or wide-bore nasogastric tube with mandatory position confirmation before use.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm indication and consent; check for contraindications (e.g. base-of-skull fracture, recent upper GI/airway surgery — seek senior advice).
Gather the NG tube, lubricant, pH indicator paper, a syringe, tape and a glass of water if the patient can swallow.
Sit the patient upright and perform hand hygiene.

steps.detail: Measure from the tip of the Nose to the Earlobe to the Xiphisternum and note the length to be inserted.
Lubricate and pass the tube along the floor of the nostril to the nasopharynx; ask the patient to swallow (sips of water) as you advance to the measured mark.

Aspirate and test on pH indicator paper — a pH of 5.5 or below confirms first-line safe (gastric) placement. If pH is above 5.5 or no aspirate is obtained, do NOT use; reposition/wait or arrange a chest X-ray per policy.
Secure the tube to the nose, document the inserted length and the confirmation method.

redFlags: NEVER use the tube for feeding/medication until gastric placement is confirmed — misplacement into the lung can be fatal.
Coughing, choking, respiratory distress or inability to speak during insertion — withdraw immediately (possible tracheal placement).
Do not pass a nasogastric tube through the nose in suspected base-of-skull fracture.

references.label: NHS Improvement / NPSA — Nasogastric tube misplacement: continuing risk of death and severe harm

title: Diagnostic lumbar puncture (adult)
summary: Sampling of cerebrospinal fluid via the lumbar subarachnoid space for diagnosis (e.g. meningitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage) using sterile technique.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm indication and consent; exclude contraindications (signs of raised intracranial pressure, coagulopathy, infection at the site).
Consider neuroimaging first if there are focal neurology, reduced consciousness or signs of raised ICP.
Gather a sterile LP pack, spinal needle, skin antiseptic, local anaesthetic, manometer and collection tubes.

steps.detail: Place in the left lateral decubitus position with the back flexed, or sitting and leaning forward; identify the L3/4 or L4/5 interspace (below the conus).
Clean the skin with antiseptic, drape, and infiltrate local anaesthetic.
Advance the spinal needle in the midline, bevel parallel to the dural fibres, until CSF flows; measure opening pressure with a manometer if indicated.
Collect CSF into the tubes in sequence, reinsert the stylet, withdraw the needle and apply a dressing.

redFlags: Do NOT perform if there are signs of raised intracranial pressure or a space-occupying lesion — risk of fatal cerebral herniation.
New leg weakness, sphincter disturbance or severe radicular pain.
Coagulopathy or therapeutic anticoagulation — correct/withhold first.

references.label: NICE NG240 — Suspected acute bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease (LP guidance)

title: Arterial blood gas (ABG) sampling
summary: Radial arterial puncture to obtain a blood sample for gas, acid-base and oxygenation analysis.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm indication and consent; assess collateral circulation (modified Allen's test) when sampling the radial artery.
Gather a pre-heparinised ABG syringe, antiseptic swab, gloves and gauze.
Perform hand hygiene; position the wrist in slight extension and palpate the radial pulse.

steps.detail: Disinfect the site, allow to dry, and palpate the artery with the non-dominant hand.
Insert the needle at roughly a 45-degree angle toward the pulse; pulsatile filling of the syringe confirms arterial access.
Allow the syringe to fill with the required volume, withdraw the needle and activate the safety device.
Apply firm pressure for several minutes (longer if anticoagulated), expel air bubbles, cap, mix and analyse promptly.

redFlags: Failed modified Allen's test (poor ulnar collateral flow) — avoid radial puncture on that side.
Persistent bleeding, expanding swelling, or signs of compartment syndrome (severe pain, pallor, paraesthesia) after puncture.
Loss of distal pulse or limb ischaemia.

references.label: WHO Guidelines on Drawing Blood — Arterial blood sampling

title: Bag-valve-mask (BVM) ventilation
summary: Manual positive-pressure ventilation using a self-inflating bag, mask and oxygen reservoir for the apnoeic or inadequately breathing patient.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Recognise inadequate breathing/apnoea; call for help.
Attach the bag-valve-mask to high-flow oxygen with a reservoir bag.
Open the airway (head tilt-chin lift, or jaw thrust if trauma); consider an oropharyngeal/nasopharyngeal airway adjunct.

steps.detail: Apply the correctly sized mask over the nose and mouth; use a two-hand 'E-C' grip with a second rescuer squeezing the bag where possible.
Deliver smooth breaths over about 1 second, each just enough to produce visible chest rise; avoid excessive volume/rate to limit gastric inflation.
Confirm chest rise, improving colour and saturation; reposition the airway or adjust the seal if ineffective.
If the patient is in cardiac arrest, coordinate ventilations with chest compressions per resuscitation guidelines.

redFlags: No chest rise despite ventilation — reposition airway, check seal and consider airway obstruction.
Gastric distension and regurgitation risk with over-vigorous ventilation.

references.label: Resuscitation Council UK — Adult Basic/Advanced Life Support guidelines

title: Selecting and applying oxygen delivery devices
summary: Choosing and applying the appropriate oxygen delivery device to achieve a prescribed target saturation.

sections.heading: Device selection
items: Nasal cannulae: low-flow oxygen (commonly 1–4 L/min) for mild requirements; comfortable, allow eating/talking.
Simple face mask: moderate oxygen needs at flows that prevent CO2 rebreathing (typically 5–10 L/min).
Venturi (fixed-performance) mask: delivers a precise FiO2, useful in patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure.
Non-rebreathe reservoir mask: high concentration oxygen for the acutely hypoxaemic/critically unwell patient at high flow.

steps.detail: Confirm oxygen is prescribed with a target saturation range and select the device accordingly.
Apply the device, set the correct flow, and check the seal/comfort and that the reservoir bag fills if used.
Adjust flow/device to keep SpO2 in the target range; step down as the patient improves.

redFlags: In patients at risk of hypercapnia, uncontrolled high-flow oxygen can cause CO2 retention — use a target range and check ABG.
Falling saturation despite a high-concentration device — escalate urgently.

references.label: BTS Guideline for oxygen use in adults in healthcare and emergency settings

title: Nebuliser therapy administration
summary: Administration of inhaled medication (e.g. bronchodilators) via a nebuliser driven by oxygen or air.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm the prescribed medication, dose and driving gas (oxygen for acute asthma; air with separate controlled oxygen for patients at risk of hypercapnia, e.g. COPD).
Assemble the nebuliser chamber, mask/mouthpiece and tubing.
Record baseline respiratory rate, SpO2 and (for asthma) peak flow if able.

steps.detail: Place the prescribed drug solution in the nebuliser chamber and attach the mask/mouthpiece.

steps.step: Set the driving gas and flow
steps.detail: Connect to the correct driving gas at a flow that produces a visible mist (commonly around 6–8 L/min) and have the patient breathe normally until the chamber is nearly dry.
Observe response and watch for side effects (tachycardia, tremor with beta-agonists).

redFlags: In COPD/hypercapnia risk, prolonged high-flow oxygen-driven nebulisation can worsen CO2 retention — drive with air and give controlled oxygen separately.
Worsening respiratory distress or exhaustion in acute asthma — escalate as life-threatening.

references.label: BTS/SIGN British Guideline on the Management of Asthma

title: Simple wound closure (suturing)
summary: Primary closure of a simple, clean traumatic wound with interrupted sutures after appropriate assessment and cleaning.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Assess the wound: mechanism, time since injury, depth, contamination, neurovascular and tendon involvement, and tetanus status.
Confirm primary closure is appropriate (avoid for grossly contaminated, infected, or high-risk bite/puncture wounds).
Gather a sterile suture pack, suture material, local anaesthetic, irrigation fluid and antiseptic.

steps.detail: Infiltrate local anaesthetic, then clean and copiously irrigate the wound; explore for foreign bodies and deep injury.
Using sterile technique, place interrupted sutures to appose wound edges without tension, everting the skin edges.
Apply a dressing, give wound-care and infection-watch advice, update tetanus prophylaxis as indicated, and arrange suture removal.

redFlags: Signs of nerve, tendon, vascular or joint involvement — refer rather than close.
Heavily contaminated or bite wounds — usually not closed primarily; consider antibiotics.
Spreading redness, pus or fever after closure — wound infection.

references.label: NICE NG42 — Tetanus / wound management (and CKS Lacerations)
WHO Surgical Care at the District Hospital (wound care)

title: Incision and drainage of a superficial abscess
summary: Surgical drainage of a localised, fluctuant superficial skin abscess to relieve symptoms and control infection.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm a fluctuant, well-localised abscess suitable for bedside drainage; assess for spreading cellulitis/systemic sepsis.
Confirm consent; gather scalpel, sterile drape, antiseptic, local anaesthetic, irrigation, packing material and dressing.
Perform hand hygiene and use aseptic technique.

steps.detail: Clean the area and infiltrate local anaesthetic around (field block) rather than into the abscess.
Make an adequate incision over the most fluctuant point along skin tension lines to allow free drainage of pus.
Express pus, break down loculations gently and irrigate the cavity; send pus for culture if indicated.
Lightly pack the cavity if needed to keep it open, apply a dressing and arrange review/repacking.

redFlags: Spreading cellulitis, systemic sepsis, or facial/hand/perianal abscesses — consider specialist referral and antibiotics.
Suspected necrotising soft tissue infection (severe pain, crepitus, rapid spread) — surgical emergency.

references.label: WHO Surgical Care at the District Hospital
NICE CKS — Boils, carbuncles and abscesses

title: Sharp wound debridement (basic)
summary: Removal of devitalised tissue, slough and debris from a wound to promote healing, within the practitioner's scope of competence.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Assess the wound and confirm debridement is indicated and within competence; identify viable versus non-viable tissue.
Assess perfusion — do not sharp-debride ischaemic or dry stable eschar on a poorly perfused limb without specialist input.
Provide analgesia and gather sterile instruments and dressings.

steps.detail: Cleanse the wound and clearly distinguish devitalised tissue from healthy granulation/structures.
Using sterile technique, conservatively remove loose slough and necrotic tissue without damaging viable tissue; stop at healthy bleeding tissue.
Achieve haemostasis and apply an appropriate dressing; consider non-sharp methods (autolytic, larval) where sharp debridement is unsuitable.

redFlags: Exposed bone, tendon, blood vessels, or unclear anatomy — refer to specialist.
Dry stable eschar on an ischaemic limb — do not debride without vascular assessment.
Uncontrolled bleeding or signs of deep/necrotising infection.

references.label: NICE — Chronic wounds: advanced wound dressings (and debridement principles)

title: Intraosseous (IO) access
summary: Establishing emergency vascular access via the bone marrow when peripheral IV access fails or is impractical in critically unwell or arrested patients.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Use when rapid vascular access is needed and IV access is delayed/failed in a critically ill or arrested patient.
Select a site (commonly proximal tibia; alternatives include distal tibia or proximal humerus), avoiding fractured or infected bones or a previously punctured bone.
Gather an IO device/needle, antiseptic, flush and the drugs/fluids to be given.

steps.detail: Identify the landmark, clean the skin with antiseptic, and use aseptic technique.
Insert the IO needle perpendicular to the bone until a give is felt on entering the marrow cavity; remove the stylet.
Confirm placement (needle stands firm, marrow aspirate or free flush); flush to confirm patency. In conscious patients, slow lidocaine flush may reduce infusion pain per protocol.
Secure the device and infuse fluids/drugs, often under pressure; replace with IV access as soon as feasible (usually within 24 hours).

redFlags: Avoid IO in a fractured bone, infected/burned overlying skin, or a previously attempted bone (risk of extravasation).
Swelling/extravasation around the site — stop infusing; risk of compartment syndrome.

references.label: Resuscitation Council UK — Advanced Life Support (vascular access)

title: Intercostal chest drain insertion
summary: Insertion of an intercostal drain to evacuate air (pneumothorax) or fluid (effusion/haemothorax/empyema) from the pleural space, using the safe triangle and a connected underwater seal.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm indication and consent (or recognise emergency/tension situation); review imaging and side.
Identify the 'safe triangle' (bordered by lateral edge of pectoralis major, lateral edge of latissimus dorsi, and a line above the level of the nipple/5th intercostal space).
Check coagulation; gather a sterile pack, drain, suture, antiseptic, local anaesthetic and an underwater seal drainage system.

steps.detail: Position the patient (arm behind head), clean and drape the safe triangle, and infiltrate local anaesthetic down to the pleura over the rib.

Make an incision and use blunt dissection just above the rib (avoiding the neurovascular bundle below the rib); enter the pleura and explore with a finger before inserting the drain (no trocar force).
Insert the drain, connect to the underwater seal and confirm swinging/bubbling; secure with a suture and dressing.
Obtain a chest X-ray to confirm position and lung re-expansion; monitor the patient and drain output.

redFlags: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical emergency — immediate needle decompression should not be delayed for imaging.
Insert above the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle; never use force/trocar (risk of organ injury).
Surgical emphysema, sudden deterioration, or large/rapid blood loss into the drain.

references.label: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline (chest drain insertion)

title: Pleural aspiration (thoracocentesis)
summary: Needle aspiration of pleural fluid for diagnosis or symptom relief, performed under ultrasound guidance where available.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm indication and consent; review imaging and check coagulation.
Use ultrasound guidance to mark or guide the optimal site for pleural fluid aspiration.
Gather sterile equipment, antiseptic, local anaesthetic, aspiration needle/cannula, syringes and specimen tubes.

steps.detail: Position the patient sitting and leaning forward; clean and drape; infiltrate local anaesthetic, inserting just above the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.
Advance the needle/cannula into the effusion while aspirating; collect fluid for the relevant diagnostic tests.
For symptom relief, remove fluid in a controlled manner; stop if the patient develops cough, chest discomfort or vasovagal symptoms.
Withdraw, dress the site, and obtain a chest X-ray afterwards (e.g. to exclude pneumothorax).

redFlags: Avoid removing very large volumes too quickly — risk of re-expansion pulmonary oedema; stop if significant cough/chest tightness develops.
Post-procedure breathlessness or pleuritic pain — suspect pneumothorax.
Insert above the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.

references.label: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline (pleural procedures)

title: Intramuscular (IM) injection
summary: Administration of medication into a muscle using a safe site and aseptic technique.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm the medication, dose, route and patient identity; check allergies.
Select an appropriate site (e.g. ventrogluteal, deltoid, vastus lateralis) and an appropriate needle length for the patient's build.
Perform hand hygiene and prepare the medication.

steps.detail: Expose and clean the site if local policy requires, allowing it to dry.
Insert the needle at 90 degrees into the muscle with a smooth motion; administer the medication at the recommended rate.
Withdraw the needle, apply gentle pressure, and dispose of the sharp directly into the sharps bin without recapping.
Observe for immediate adverse/allergic reactions, especially after vaccines or first-time medications.

redFlags: Signs of anaphylaxis after injection (urticaria, wheeze, swelling, hypotension) — treat as an emergency.
Avoid injecting into infected/inflamed skin or near major nerves/vessels.

references.label: WHO Best Practices for Injections and Related Procedures Toolkit

title: Subcutaneous (SC) injection
summary: Administration of medication (e.g. insulin, low-molecular-weight heparin) into subcutaneous tissue.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm the medication, dose, route and patient identity; check allergies.
Select a site with adequate subcutaneous tissue (e.g. abdomen, outer thigh, upper arm) and rotate sites for repeated injections.
Perform hand hygiene and prepare the medication.

steps.detail: Clean the site if policy requires and allow to dry; pinch a skin fold if needed.
Insert the needle (commonly at 45–90 degrees depending on needle length and tissue) and administer the medication slowly.
Withdraw the needle, apply gentle pressure (do not rub heparin sites), and dispose of the sharp safely.

redFlags: Signs of allergic reaction after injection — treat appropriately.
Avoid bruised, infected or lipohypertrophied sites.

references.label: WHO Best Practices for Injections and Related Procedures Toolkit

title: WHO 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene
summary: The WHO 'My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene' framework defines the key times during care when hand hygiene must be performed to interrupt transmission of healthcare-associated pathogens.

steps.detail: Perform hand hygiene before approaching/touching the patient to protect them from harmful germs carried on your hands.
Immediately before any clean/aseptic task (e.g. wound care, IV access) to protect the patient from germs entering their body.
Immediately after an exposure risk to body fluids and after glove removal, to protect yourself and the environment.
After touching the patient and their immediate surroundings, when leaving the patient's side.
After touching any object/furniture in the patient's immediate surroundings, even without touching the patient.

sections.heading: Technique
items: Use alcohol-based handrub for routine decontamination of visibly clean hands; wash with soap and water when hands are visibly soiled or after caring for patients with spore-forming organisms (e.g. C. difficile).
Cover all surfaces of the hands and rub/wash for the recommended duration.

references.label: WHO Guidelines on Hand Hygiene in Health Care — My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene

redFlags: Outbreak setting with rising hand-hygiene non-compliance audits — escalate to IPC team.
Visible soiling, body fluid contamination or known C. difficile / norovirus — use soap-and-water hand wash, not alcohol gel.
Skin breakdown / dermatitis preventing alcohol gel use — refer to occupational health for skin-care plan.

title: Standard precautions
summary: Standard precautions are the minimum infection prevention practices that apply to the care of all patients, regardless of suspected or confirmed infection status.

sections.heading: Core elements
items: Hand hygiene at the appropriate moments.
Use of personal protective equipment based on anticipated exposure (gloves, gown/apron, mask, eye protection).
Respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette.
Safe injection practices and safe handling/disposal of sharps.
Safe handling of potentially contaminated equipment and environmental cleaning.
Safe management of linen, waste and spills of blood/body fluids.

sections.heading: Application
items: Treat all blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions (except sweat), non-intact skin and mucous membranes as potentially infectious.
Apply at all times to all patients in addition to any transmission-based precautions.

references.label: WHO — Standard precautions in health care
CDC — Standard Precautions for All Patient Care

redFlags: Aerosol-generating procedure planned (intubation, bronchoscopy, suctioning) — escalate to airborne precautions.
Sharps injury / mucocutaneous blood exposure — initiate post-exposure protocol and report immediately.
Uncertainty about pathogen — adopt the most protective transmission-based precaution until clarified.

title: PPE donning and doffing sequence
summary: The correct sequence for putting on (donning) and removing (doffing) personal protective equipment to minimise self-contamination.

steps.detail: Put on the gown, covering the torso from neck to knees and arms to the wrists; fasten at the back.
Secure the mask/respirator, fit the flexible band to the nose bridge and ensure a snug fit (fit-check a respirator).
Place goggles or a face shield over the eyes/face and adjust to fit.
Put on gloves, extending them to cover the cuff of the gown.
Remove gloves first (most contaminated) using a glove-to-glove then skin-to-skin technique; perform hand hygiene.
Remove goggles/face shield from the back (the front is contaminated).
Unfasten and remove the gown, rolling it away from the body, contaminated side inward.
Remove last by grasping the ties/elastics (not the front); perform hand hygiene immediately afterwards.

redFlags: Improper doffing is a leading cause of self-contamination — perform hand hygiene between and after steps.

references.label: CDC — Sequence for Putting On and Removing Personal Protective Equipment

title: Contact precautions
summary: Transmission-based precautions for organisms spread by direct or indirect contact (e.g. MRSA, multidrug-resistant organisms, C. difficile).

sections.heading: Precautions
items: Place the patient in a single room where possible, or cohort with patients with the same organism.
Wear gloves and a gown/apron for contact with the patient or their environment.
Perform hand hygiene before and after contact; for C. difficile and other spore-forming organisms, wash with soap and water (alcohol handrub does not kill spores).
Use dedicated or single-use patient equipment, and clean/disinfect shared equipment between patients.

sections.heading: Environment
items: Enhance environmental cleaning of the room and high-touch surfaces.
Limit patient transport; communicate precautions when transfer is necessary.

references.label: CDC — Transmission-Based Precautions (Contact)

redFlags: MRSA / VRE / multi-drug-resistant Gram-negative outbreak — notify IPC for cohorting.
Patient with continuous diarrhoea or open uncontained wound — reinforce single-room placement.
C. difficile suspected — switch from alcohol gel to soap-and-water hand hygiene and use sporicidal cleaning.

title: Droplet precautions
summary: Transmission-based precautions for organisms spread by respiratory droplets over short distances (e.g. influenza, pertussis, meningococcus).

sections.heading: Precautions
items: Place the patient in a single room where possible, or cohort.
Wear a surgical (fluid-resistant) mask when within close distance of the patient.
Add eye protection where splashes/sprays are anticipated, and apply standard precautions.
Perform hand hygiene at the appropriate moments.

sections.heading: Patient measures
items: Have the patient wear a surgical mask during transport, and encourage respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette.
Limit patient movement out of the room.

references.label: CDC — Transmission-Based Precautions (Droplet)

redFlags: Confirmed or suspected emerging respiratory pathogen — escalate to airborne precautions pending IPC guidance.
Patient unable to wear a surgical mask during transport — defer transport unless clinically urgent.
Healthcare worker without correctly fitted surgical mask — pause patient contact and re-fit.

title: Airborne precautions
summary: Transmission-based precautions for organisms that remain infectious over long distances when suspended in the air (e.g. tuberculosis, measles, varicella).

sections.heading: Precautions
items: Place the patient in an airborne infection isolation room (negative-pressure, where available) with the door kept closed.
Wear a fit-tested particulate respirator (e.g. N95/FFP2 or higher as indicated) before entering the room.
Limit the number of staff entering and apply standard precautions.
Perform hand hygiene at the appropriate moments.

sections.heading: Patient measures
items: Have the patient wear a surgical mask during any necessary transport.
Minimise transport and aerosol-generating procedures; use additional protection for the latter.

references.label: CDC — Transmission-Based Precautions (Airborne)
WHO — Infection prevention and control of tuberculosis

redFlags: Negative-pressure room unavailable for confirmed pulmonary TB / measles / varicella — relocate or arrange transfer.
N95 / FFP3 fit-test failure or seal break during use — leave the room and replace before re-entry.
Aerosol-generating procedure outside a negative-pressure room — defer or escalate to anaesthesia / ICU.

title: Sharps safety and injury management
summary: Safe handling and disposal of sharps to prevent needlestick injuries and bloodborne virus transmission, and immediate management after an exposure.

sections.heading: Prevention
items: Do not recap, bend or break needles by hand; use safety-engineered devices where available.
Dispose of sharps immediately into a puncture-resistant sharps container at the point of use.
Do not overfill sharps containers (close at the fill line).
Use standard precautions and PPE during procedures involving sharps.

steps.detail: Encourage the wound to bleed gently and wash with soap and running water; do not scrub. Irrigate mucous membranes/eyes with water/saline.
Report immediately per local policy and seek urgent occupational health/clinical assessment of the source and recipient.
Risk-assess for bloodborne viruses and start post-exposure prophylaxis (e.g. for HIV) promptly where indicated, and consider hepatitis B measures.

redFlags: A high-risk source exposure (e.g. HIV) requires urgent assessment — HIV PEP is most effective when started as soon as possible after exposure.

references.label: WHO — Health worker safety / injection safety

title: Central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) prevention bundle
summary: Evidence-based insertion and maintenance bundle to prevent CLABSI in patients with central venous catheters.

sections.heading: Insertion bundle
items: Perform hand hygiene before insertion.
Use maximal sterile barrier precautions (cap, mask, sterile gown and gloves, full-body sterile drape).
Use a chlorhexidine-based skin antiseptic and allow it to dry.
Select an optimal site (avoid the femoral vein in adults where possible).
Use a checklist and empower staff to stop insertion if asepsis is breached.

sections.heading: Maintenance bundle
items: Review the need for the line daily and remove it promptly when no longer required.
Perform hand hygiene and disinfect hubs/connectors before every access.
Maintain a clean, intact dressing; change per policy (gauze approximately every 48 hours, transparent up to every 7 days, or sooner if soiled/loose).

references.label: CDC — Guidelines for the Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections

redFlags: Bundle compliance audit < 95% — escalate to IPC and unit leadership for root-cause analysis.
New fever with central line in place — review for line removal or paired blood cultures (peripheral + line).
Local erythema, purulence or tunnel infection — remove line and send tip for culture.

title: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) prevention bundle
summary: Bundle to reduce CAUTI by avoiding unnecessary catheterisation, using aseptic insertion, and maintaining a closed drainage system.

sections.heading: Bundle elements
items: Insert urinary catheters only for appropriate clinical indications and document the reason.
Insert using aseptic technique and sterile equipment.
Maintain a closed drainage system; keep the bag below bladder level and off the floor.
Perform hand hygiene before and after any catheter manipulation.
Review the need for the catheter daily and remove it as soon as it is no longer required.
Provide routine daily meatal hygiene (soap and water).

references.label: CDC — Guideline for Prevention of Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections
NICE QS61 — urinary catheters

redFlags: Catheter in place > 48 h without ongoing indication — escalate to medical team for removal.
New fever, suprapubic pain or visible cloudy / haematuria — re-evaluate for symptomatic CAUTI and consider line change.
Outbreak of multi-drug-resistant urinary organisms — notify IPC for cohorting and review of catheter care.

title: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) prevention bundle
summary: Care bundle to reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia in mechanically ventilated patients.

sections.heading: Bundle elements
items: Elevate the head of the bed to 30–45 degrees unless contraindicated.
Perform daily sedation interruption ('sedation holds') and daily assessment of readiness to extubate.
Provide regular oral care (e.g. with chlorhexidine per local policy).
Provide peptic ulcer (stress ulcer) prophylaxis as indicated.
Provide venous thromboembolism prophylaxis as indicated.
Maintain endotracheal cuff pressure and consider subglottic secretion drainage.

references.label: IHI — Ventilator Bundle / How-to Guide: Prevent Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia

redFlags: Bundle compliance < 95% (head-of-bed, sedation interruption, oral care, DVT and stress-ulcer prophylaxis) — escalate.
New fever with rising secretions or worsening oxygenation in a ventilated patient — investigate for VAP.
Unplanned extubation followed by re-intubation — escalate to ICU lead for root-cause review.

title: Surgical site infection (SSI) prevention
summary: Perioperative measures recommended by WHO to reduce surgical site infections.

sections.heading: Pre-operative
items: Patients should bathe/shower before surgery.
Do not remove hair, or if necessary remove with clippers (never shave with a razor).
Administer surgical antibiotic prophylaxis within the recommended time window before incision, when indicated.
Use an alcohol-based chlorhexidine skin preparation for surgical site antisepsis.

sections.heading: Intra- and post-operative
items: Maintain optimal oxygenation, normothermia and glycaemic control perioperatively.
Do not continue surgical antibiotic prophylaxis after wound closure for the purpose of preventing SSI.
Use appropriate surgical hand preparation and maintain sterile technique.

references.label: WHO — Global Guidelines for the Prevention of Surgical Site Infection
NICE NG125 — Surgical site infections: prevention and treatment

redFlags: Pre-operative MRSA / S. aureus screen positive without decolonisation — escalate to surgical team.
Hyperglycaemia (BG > 11 mmol/L) intra-operatively — escalate to anaesthesia.
Surgical wound dehiscence or purulent discharge < 30 days postoperatively — review for SSI and culture.

title: Tuberculosis airborne infection control
summary: Administrative, environmental and respiratory protection measures to prevent transmission of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in healthcare settings.

sections.heading: Administrative controls
items: Promptly identify, separate (in a designated area) and prioritise people with presumptive/confirmed infectious TB to minimise time in shared spaces.
Promote cough etiquette and provide masks for patients with respiratory symptoms.
Investigate and start effective treatment quickly, which reduces infectiousness.

sections.heading: Environmental and respiratory protection
items: Use adequate ventilation (natural or mechanical) and, where available, airborne infection isolation rooms.
Healthcare workers should wear fit-tested particulate respirators when caring for patients with infectious or drug-resistant TB and during aerosol-generating procedures.
Maintain hand hygiene and standard precautions.

redFlags: Suspected drug-resistant TB or a patient undergoing aerosol-generating procedures — heightened airborne protection required.

references.label: WHO — Guidelines on tuberculosis infection prevention and control

title: Viral haemorrhagic fever / Ebola IPC precautions
summary: Infection prevention and control measures when caring for patients with suspected or confirmed filovirus disease (e.g. Ebola, Marburg) and other viral haemorrhagic fevers.

sections.heading: Core precautions
items: Apply standard precautions plus contact and droplet precautions for all patients at all times.
Isolate suspected/confirmed cases in a dedicated single room/area with restricted, trained staff.
Use full recommended PPE (impermeable gown/coverall, double gloves, fluid-resistant mask, eye protection/face shield, head and foot cover) appropriate to the level of care.
Perform PPE donning and doffing under supervision (a trained observer) using the prescribed sequence.

sections.heading: Additional measures
items: Use safe injection practices and minimise invasive procedures.
Practise safe handling of blood/body fluids, waste, linen and the deceased (safe and dignified burial).
Strict hand hygiene and environmental disinfection with an appropriate chlorine-based or approved disinfectant.

redFlags: Any breach in PPE or potential exposure to body fluids — report immediately for risk assessment and monitoring.

references.label: WHO — Infection prevention and control for Ebola/Marburg virus disease

title: Environmental cleaning and disinfection
summary: Routine and targeted cleaning of the healthcare environment to reduce the burden of pathogens on surfaces and equipment.

sections.heading: Principles
items: Clean from cleanest to dirtiest and from high to low surfaces to avoid recontamination.
Prioritise frequent cleaning of high-touch surfaces (bed rails, call bells, door handles, monitors).
Use the correct detergent/disinfectant at the correct concentration and contact time per local policy.
Use colour-coded or dedicated cleaning equipment to avoid cross-contamination between areas.

sections.heading: Targeted cleaning
items: Enhance cleaning/disinfection for rooms of patients on transmission-based precautions.
For C. difficile and other spore-forming organisms, use a sporicidal agent (e.g. chlorine-based) per policy.
Manage blood/body-fluid spills promptly using the recommended procedure.

references.label: WHO — Environmental cleaning and infection prevention and control
CDC — Environmental cleaning procedures

redFlags: Cluster of healthcare-associated infections — escalate environmental sampling and review cleaning protocol.
Spillage of blood or body fluids — escalate to spill-response protocol (sodium hypochlorite 10 000 ppm).
Visible contamination after cleaning — re-clean before bed allocation.

title: Isolation precautions: choosing the right type
summary: Overview of how to select transmission-based precautions (contact, droplet, airborne) in addition to standard precautions, based on the route of transmission.

sections.heading: Selecting precautions by route
items: Always apply standard precautions for every patient.
Contact precautions: organisms spread by direct/indirect contact (e.g. MRSA, MDROs, C. difficile, scabies) — gloves and gown, single room.
Droplet precautions: organisms spread by respiratory droplets (e.g. influenza, pertussis, meningococcus) — surgical mask within close range, single room.
Airborne precautions: organisms suspended in air over distance (e.g. TB, measles, varicella) — fit-tested respirator and negative-pressure room.

sections.heading: General measures
items: Some conditions require combined precautions (e.g. some respiratory viruses).
Communicate precautions clearly (signage), limit patient transport, and educate visitors.
Discontinue precautions per criteria when the patient is no longer infectious.

references.label: CDC — 2007 Guideline for Isolation Precautions / Transmission-Based Precautions

redFlags: Pathogen identity unclear — adopt the most protective precaution combination (contact + droplet ± airborne) until clarified.
High-consequence infectious disease suspected (VHF, monkeypox, novel respiratory) — notify IPC and public-health immediately.
Inability to provide single-room isolation — escalate to bed-management and IPC for cohorting plan.

title: Healthcare outbreak response basics
summary: Initial steps for recognising and responding to a suspected healthcare-associated outbreak.

sections.heading: Recognition and notification
items: Recognise an outbreak (a greater-than-expected number of cases of an infection linked in time/place).
Notify the infection prevention and control team and relevant public health authority promptly.
Apply or escalate transmission-based precautions immediately for affected and at-risk patients.

steps.detail: Agree a case definition and actively find cases; collect specimens for laboratory confirmation.
Reinforce hand hygiene, cohort patients/staff, enhance cleaning, and review IPC practices; restrict transfers/admissions if advised.
Investigate source and transmission, document a line list, and communicate with staff, patients and management.
Monitor for new cases and stand down measures when criteria are met.

references.label: WHO — Outbreak management and IPC

redFlags: Two or more linked cases of the same syndrome on the same unit within the typical incubation window — declare a possible outbreak.
Cluster of severe disease, deaths, or healthcare-worker illness — escalate to local public-health authority.
Suspected high-consequence pathogen — immediate IPC and public-health notification.

title: Maintenance IV fluids (adults)
summary: Routine maintenance intravenous fluid prescribing for adults who cannot meet needs orally, following NICE CG174.

sections.heading: Routine maintenance requirements
items: Water: approximately 25–30 mL/kg/day.
Sodium, potassium and chloride: approximately 1 mmol/kg/day each.
Glucose: approximately 50–100 g/day to limit starvation ketosis (this is not full nutrition).
NICE suggests considering using 25–30 mL/kg/day of sodium chloride 0.18% in 4% glucose with potassium as a starting point for routine maintenance.

steps.detail: Base calculations on ideal body weight; prescribe less for older, frail, renal or cardiac-failure patients (e.g. consider 20–25 mL/kg/day) and reassess.
Use pre-mixed potassium-containing bags — NEVER add potassium to an IV bag on the ward.
Review fluids at least daily, monitor weight, fluid balance and U&Es, and switch to oral fluids as soon as possible.

redFlags: Never add potassium to infusion bags manually — concentrated potassium administration can be fatal.
Watch for fluid overload (oedema, breathlessness) especially in heart/renal failure and the elderly.
Hyponatraemia from inappropriate hypotonic fluids — monitor sodium.

references.label: NICE CG174 — Intravenous fluid therapy in adults in hospital

title: Fluid resuscitation bolus (adults)
summary: Intravenous fluid resuscitation for the hypovolaemic/shocked adult per NICE CG174.

sections.heading: Resuscitation approach
items: Identify the need for resuscitation: clinical signs of hypovolaemia/shock (e.g. tachycardia, hypotension, prolonged capillary refill, reduced urine output, raised lactate).
Use a crystalloid containing sodium in the range 130–154 mmol/L.
Give a fluid bolus of 500 mL over less than 15 minutes.

steps.detail: Reassess the patient after each bolus for response and signs of overload.
Give further boluses (typically up to a total around 2000 mL) reassessing each time; seek expert help if more is required or there is no response.
Identify and treat the underlying cause (e.g. haemorrhage, sepsis) alongside resuscitation.

redFlags: No improvement after repeated boluses, or signs of fluid overload — escalate to senior/critical care urgently.
Suspected haemorrhagic shock — control bleeding and consider blood products rather than large-volume crystalloid.

references.label: NICE CG174 — Intravenous fluid therapy in adults in hospital

title: Fluid resuscitation bolus (paediatric)
summary: Initial fluid resuscitation for the shocked child using weight-based isotonic crystalloid boluses with reassessment.

sections.heading: Resuscitation approach
items: Use an isotonic crystalloid (e.g. 0.9% sodium chloride or balanced solution).
Give a bolus of 10–20 mL/kg, reassessing after each bolus (use 10 mL/kg in conditions such as DKA, trauma, cardiac failure, and in neonates).
In low-resource/WHO settings without intensive care, use cautious boluses and reassess frequently for fluid overload.

steps.detail: Reassess heart rate, perfusion, conscious level and signs of overload (e.g. crackles, hepatomegaly, gallop) after every bolus.
Repeat boluses as needed while seeking senior/critical care help; stop fluids if signs of overload develop.
Treat the underlying cause (e.g. sepsis) and start maintenance fluids once resuscitated.

redFlags: Signs of fluid overload (respiratory distress, hepatomegaly, gallop rhythm) — stop boluses and reassess.
No response after repeated boluses — escalate urgently; consider inotropes/critical care.

references.label: WHO — Updated guideline: paediatric emergency triage, assessment and treatment
Resuscitation Council UK — Paediatric Advanced Life Support

title: WHO ORS dehydration treatment plans (A/B/C)
summary: WHO classification of dehydration in diarrhoeal illness and the corresponding treatment plans A (no dehydration), B (some dehydration) and C (severe dehydration).

sections.heading: Plan A — no dehydration (home management)
items: Give extra fluids and ORS after each loose stool to prevent dehydration; continue feeding/breastfeeding.
Give zinc supplementation as recommended.
Advise carers when to return (signs of dehydration, blood in stool, not improving).

steps.detail: Give approximately 75 mL/kg of low-osmolarity ORS over 4 hours under observation; give frequent small sips and continue breastfeeding.
Reassess hydration and reclassify: if improved to no dehydration use Plan A; if some dehydration persists repeat Plan B; if severe, move to Plan C.

Start IV Ringer's lactate (or normal saline) immediately, totalling 100 mL/kg, divided by age (e.g. infants <12 months: 30 mL/kg over 1 hour then 70 mL/kg over 5 hours; children ≥12 months: 30 mL/kg over 30 minutes then 70 mL/kg over 2.5 hours).
Reassess and give ORS as soon as the child can drink; reassess and adjust according to response.

redFlags: Severe dehydration (lethargy/unconscious, sunken eyes, very slow skin pinch, unable to drink) — start IV fluids immediately (Plan C).
Blood in stool, persistent vomiting, or failure to improve — reassess for other causes.

references.label: WHO — The Treatment of Diarrhoea: a manual for physicians and other senior health workers

title: Clinical assessment of dehydration
summary: Clinical assessment to classify the degree of dehydration and guide the appropriate WHO treatment plan.

sections.heading: Assessment signs
items: General condition: alert (none), restless/irritable (some), lethargic/unconscious (severe).
Eyes: normal, sunken, very sunken.
Thirst: drinks normally, drinks eagerly/thirsty, drinks poorly or unable to drink.
Skin pinch: goes back quickly, goes back slowly, goes back very slowly (>2 seconds).

sections.heading: Classification
items: No dehydration: not enough signs to classify as some/severe — manage with Plan A.
Some dehydration: two or more signs including restlessness/irritability, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly, slow skin pinch — manage with Plan B.
Severe dehydration: two or more signs including lethargy/unconsciousness, very sunken eyes, unable to drink, very slow skin pinch — manage with Plan C urgently.

redFlags: Severe dehydration or shock (cold extremities, weak/absent pulses, prolonged capillary refill) — treat as an emergency.
Inability to drink/breastfeed or lethargy — severe category.

references.label: WHO — The Treatment of Diarrhoea: a manual for physicians and other senior health workers

title: Hyperkalaemia emergency management (adults)
summary: Emergency treatment of severe hyperkalaemia in adults, prioritising cardiac membrane protection and shifting potassium intracellularly, then removal.

sections.heading: Assess severity
items: Confirm true hyperkalaemia (exclude haemolysed/spurious sample) and obtain an urgent ECG.
Severe hyperkalaemia is generally serum potassium 6.5 mmol/L or above, or any level with ECG changes.
ECG changes (peaked T waves, broad QRS, loss of P waves, sine wave) indicate imminent cardiac risk.

steps.detail: If ECG changes are present, give IV calcium (e.g. 10% calcium gluconate) to stabilise the cardiac membrane; repeat if ECG changes persist. This does not lower potassium.

Give insulin with glucose (commonly 10 units soluble insulin in glucose) — the most effective shifting therapy; monitor blood glucose closely and give a 10% glucose infusion afterwards if pre-treatment glucose is low to prevent hypoglycaemia. Nebulised salbutamol is an additional shifting agent.
Consider a potassium binder; arrange dialysis for refractory or severe hyperkalaemia, especially with renal failure.
Recheck potassium and glucose regularly; treat the underlying cause and stop contributing drugs/potassium intake.

redFlags: Any ECG change with hyperkalaemia is a medical emergency — give IV calcium immediately and call for senior help.
Risk of hypoglycaemia after insulin-glucose treatment — monitor glucose for several hours.
Refractory hyperkalaemia or anuria — urgent dialysis.

references.label: UK Kidney Association — Clinical Practice Guideline: Treatment of Acute Hyperkalaemia in Adults

title: Hypokalaemia potassium replacement (adults)
summary: Safe correction of low serum potassium, choosing oral versus IV replacement and capping IV infusion rates.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Confirm the level and assess severity and symptoms (weakness, arrhythmia); obtain an ECG (e.g. U waves, flattened T waves).
Check magnesium — hypokalaemia is difficult to correct while hypomagnesaemic; replace magnesium too.
Identify the cause (GI losses, diuretics, renal losses, shift).

steps.detail: For mild/moderate hypokalaemia in a patient who can take oral, use oral potassium supplements.
Use pre-prepared potassium-containing IV fluids; on a general ward the IV infusion rate should not exceed 10 mmol/hour, and a peripheral concentration of about 40 mmol/L is usual.

steps.step: Use monitored, central access for higher rates
steps.detail: Faster rates or higher concentrations require cardiac monitoring and central access in a critical-care setting.
Recheck potassium during and after replacement and continue treating the cause.

redFlags: NEVER give undiluted/rapid IV potassium or bolus potassium — this can cause fatal arrhythmia.
Severe symptomatic hypokalaemia with arrhythmia — manage with cardiac monitoring in a high-care setting.

references.label: BNF — Fluids and electrolytes: potassium imbalance

title: Hyponatraemia correction (adults)
summary: Assessment and controlled correction of hyponatraemia, with rate caps to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Assess severity of symptoms and chronicity; severe symptoms (seizures, reduced consciousness, vomiting) indicate emergency treatment.
Assess volume status (hypovolaemic, euvolaemic, hypervolaemic) to guide management.
Review medications and likely cause (e.g. SIADH, diuretics, heart/liver/renal failure).

steps.detail: For severe symptomatic hyponatraemia, give hypertonic (3%) saline as a bolus per protocol, in a monitored setting, aiming for a small rapid rise (about 4–6 mmol/L) to control symptoms.
Limit the rise in serum sodium to no more than about 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours (some experts use a stricter 8 mmol/L limit), and about 18 mmol/L over 48 hours, to avoid osmotic demyelination.
Manage according to volume status (e.g. fluid restriction in SIADH, careful saline in hypovolaemia); avoid over-rapid correction.
Recheck sodium frequently; if correction is too fast, relowering with hypotonic fluids/desmopressin may be needed per specialist advice.

redFlags: Over-rapid correction can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome (delayed, often irreversible neurological injury) — adhere to rate caps.
Severe symptoms (seizures, coma) — emergency; treat with hypertonic saline under senior supervision.

references.label: European clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia

title: Hypernatraemia management (adults)
summary: Correction of high serum sodium by addressing water deficit and the underlying cause, with a controlled rate to avoid cerebral oedema.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Assess volume status and the cause (water loss, reduced intake, sodium gain, diabetes insipidus).
Assess for symptoms (thirst, confusion, irritability, seizures in severe cases).
Estimate the free water deficit to guide replacement.

steps.detail: If hypovolaemic/shocked, restore intravascular volume with isotonic fluid before focusing on free-water replacement.
Replace the water deficit using the oral/enteral route where possible, or IV hypotonic fluid (e.g. 5% glucose or 0.45% saline) as appropriate.
Lower serum sodium gradually (commonly no faster than about 10 mmol/L per 24 hours, slower in chronic cases) to avoid cerebral oedema.
Treat the underlying cause (e.g. desmopressin for cranial diabetes insipidus) and recheck sodium regularly.

redFlags: Over-rapid lowering of sodium can cause cerebral oedema and seizures — correct gradually.
Severe hypernatraemia with reduced consciousness or seizures — senior/critical-care input.

references.label: BNF / NICE CKS — Hypernatraemia and fluid management

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) fluid and insulin protocol (adults)
summary: Emergency management of DKA in adults focusing on IV fluid replacement, fixed-rate insulin and potassium monitoring, per JBDS guidance.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and initial fluids
items: Diagnose DKA on the triad of ketonaemia/ketonuria, hyperglycaemia (or known diabetes), and acidosis (bicarbonate low / venous pH low).
Start IV 0.9% sodium chloride; if systolic BP is below 90 mmHg give 500 mL over 10–15 minutes and repeat if needed, then continue a structured replacement regimen.
Assess for and treat any precipitant (e.g. infection, missed insulin).

steps.detail: Start a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour; continue the patient's usual long-acting insulin.
When blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L, add 10% glucose alongside the saline; consider reducing the insulin rate to 0.05 units/kg/hour to reduce hypoglycaemia/hypokalaemia risk.
Add potassium to fluids guided by serum potassium (insulin drives potassium into cells); do not add potassium if potassium is high or the patient is anuric. Use pre-mixed bags only.
Monitor glucose, ketones, potassium and pH/bicarbonate hourly initially; aim to clear ketones and resolve acidosis.

redFlags: Hypokalaemia during treatment can be fatal — monitor potassium closely once insulin is started.
