Reduced consciousness, suspected cerebral oedema (especially younger patients), or shock — escalate to critical care.
Failure of ketones/acidosis to improve — reassess insulin delivery and precipitant.

references.label: JBDS — The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults (revised 2023)

title: Hypomagnesaemia replacement (adults)
summary: Recognition and replacement of low serum magnesium, which often coexists with and impairs correction of hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Assess for symptoms (weakness, tremor, arrhythmias) and check an ECG.
Recognise that hypomagnesaemia frequently accompanies hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia and can make them refractory.
Identify the cause (GI losses, alcohol, diuretics, proton pump inhibitors, refeeding).

steps.detail: For severe/symptomatic hypomagnesaemia, give IV magnesium sulfate; for mild/asymptomatic cases use oral magnesium salts (limited by diarrhoea).
Replace magnesium to enable effective correction of potassium and calcium.
Give IV magnesium as a controlled infusion per protocol with monitoring; recheck levels and treat the cause.

redFlags: Severe hypomagnesaemia with arrhythmia or seizures — emergency IV replacement with cardiac monitoring.
Refractory hypokalaemia/hypocalcaemia — check and replace magnesium.

references.label: BNF — Magnesium imbalance

title: Hypocalcaemia management (adults)
summary: Recognition and treatment of low calcium, distinguishing acute symptomatic hypocalcaemia (an emergency) from chronic mild hypocalcaemia.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Use the corrected (albumin-adjusted) or ionised calcium.
Assess for neuromuscular irritability: paraesthesia, tetany, Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs, and in severe cases seizures or arrhythmia (prolonged QT).
Identify the cause (e.g. hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, hypomagnesaemia, post-thyroid/parathyroid surgery).

steps.detail: Give IV calcium (e.g. calcium gluconate) for severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia (tetany, seizures, arrhythmia), diluted and infused per protocol with cardiac monitoring.
Check and correct hypomagnesaemia, which can cause refractory hypocalcaemia.
Use oral calcium and vitamin D (e.g. activated vitamin D) for mild or chronic hypocalcaemia; treat the underlying cause.
Recheck calcium (and ECG where relevant) and adjust treatment.

redFlags: Tetany, seizures, laryngospasm or arrhythmia (prolonged QT) — emergency IV calcium with cardiac monitoring.
Refractory hypocalcaemia — check and correct magnesium.

references.label: Society for Endocrinology — Emergency management of acute hypocalcaemia in adults

title: Refeeding syndrome prevention and management
summary: Identification of patients at risk of refeeding syndrome and safe reintroduction of nutrition with electrolyte and vitamin support, per NICE CG32.

sections.heading: Identify those at risk
items: High risk if one or more of: BMI under 16 kg/m2, unintentional weight loss >15% in 3–6 months, little/no nutritional intake for >10 days, or low potassium/phosphate/magnesium before feeding.

Or two or more of: BMI under 18.5 kg/m2, weight loss >10% in 3–6 months, little/no intake for >5 days, or a history of alcohol/drug misuse or certain drugs (insulin, chemotherapy, antacids, diuretics).
Check baseline potassium, phosphate, magnesium and other electrolytes.

steps.detail: In high-risk patients, start nutrition at a low rate (NICE: start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day, or 5 kcal/kg/day in extreme cases) and increase slowly over days to meet full needs.
Give thiamine and other B vitamins and a balanced multivitamin/trace element supplement before and during the first days of feeding.
Monitor and correct potassium, phosphate and magnesium; provide supplementation as needed during refeeding.
Monitor electrolytes, fluid balance and clinical status closely during the early refeeding period.

redFlags: Falling phosphate, potassium or magnesium after starting feeding — hallmark of refeeding syndrome; can cause arrhythmia and cardiac/respiratory failure.
Cardiac, neurological or respiratory deterioration during refeeding — escalate.

references.label: NICE CG32 — Nutrition support for adults (refeeding syndrome)

title: Tracheostomy care nursing care plan
summary: Ongoing nursing care of a patient with a tracheostomy, including airway humidification, suctioning, stoma and inner-cannula care, and emergency preparedness for tube displacement or blockage.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Confirm tube type, size, whether cuffed and the date/reason for insertion; document at the bedside.
Ensure emergency equipment is at the bedside at all times: a spare tube of the same size, a spare tube one size smaller, a 10 mL syringe, tracheal dilators/obturator, suction and a bag-valve device.
Assess respiratory rate, SpO2, work of breathing, secretion volume/character and stoma site condition.

steps.detail: Provide continuous humidification (the upper airway is bypassed) to prevent secretions thickening and tube blockage.
Suction only when needed (not routinely), using an appropriately sized catheter and aseptic technique, pre-oxygenating and limiting each pass to avoid hypoxia and trauma.

steps.step: Care for the inner cannula and stoma
steps.detail: Inspect/clean or change the inner cannula regularly per type, and clean and dress the stoma to prevent skin breakdown and infection.
Monitor cuff pressure where applicable and ensure tube ties are secure but allow one finger underneath.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Document suction, stoma care, inner-cannula care and respiratory status each shift.
Ensure all staff can follow the emergency tracheostomy/laryngectomy algorithm.

redFlags: Tube blockage or displacement causing respiratory distress, low SpO2 or inability to ventilate — call for help and follow the emergency tracheostomy algorithm immediately.
Bleeding from the stoma, surgical emphysema, or signs of tracheo-innominate fistula (sentinel pulsatile bleed) — emergency.
A laryngectomy patient has no upper-airway connection — oxygenate via the stoma, not the mouth/nose.

references.label: National Tracheostomy Safety Project — emergency management resources

title: Stoma (colostomy/ileostomy/urostomy) care nursing care plan
summary: Nursing care of a patient with a bowel or urinary stoma, including stoma and peristomal skin assessment, appliance management, output monitoring and patient self-care education.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Assess stoma colour (should be pink/red and moist), size, height and type (colostomy, ileostomy, urostomy).
Inspect peristomal skin for excoriation, soreness or leakage and assess appliance fit.
Monitor output: volume, consistency and colour; ileostomy/urostomy output is higher and more fluid.

steps.detail: Measure the stoma and cut the baseplate to fit snugly, protecting peristomal skin; empty/change the appliance before it is over-full to prevent leakage.
Clean with water, dry thoroughly and use barrier products only as needed; treat skin breakdown promptly.
Watch for high-output stoma (especially ileostomy) leading to dehydration and electrolyte loss; record intake/output.
Teach the patient to manage the appliance and recognise complications; involve the stoma care nurse and address psychological adjustment.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Document stoma appearance, output and skin condition.
Refer to the specialist stoma nurse for complications or education needs.

redFlags: Dusky, dark or black stoma — suspect ischaemia/necrosis; escalate urgently.
High-output stoma with signs of dehydration/electrolyte disturbance.
No output with distension, pain and vomiting — suspect obstruction.

references.label: Association of Stoma Care Nurses UK — clinical guidelines

title: Chest drain observation and management nursing care plan
summary: Nursing care and observation of a patient with an intercostal chest drain, including drainage monitoring, recognition of swinging/bubbling and prevention of complications.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Confirm the indication (pneumothorax, effusion, haemothorax, empyema) and drain insertion details.
Observe the underwater seal: 'swinging' (oscillation with respiration) indicates patency; 'bubbling' indicates an air leak.
Assess respiratory rate, SpO2, work of breathing, drain site and the volume/character of drainage.

steps.step: Keep the system below the chest
steps.detail: Keep the drainage bottle upright and below the level of the patient's chest at all times to maintain the underwater seal and prevent backflow.
Do not clamp a bubbling chest drain (risk of tension pneumothorax); follow local policy if clamping is ever indicated and seek senior advice.
Apply suction only if prescribed; check tubing is not kinked and the seal is intact; never lift the bottle above the insertion site.

steps.step: Care for the site and patient
steps.detail: Inspect the dressing, support mobility and analgesia, and encourage deep breathing.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Record drainage volume, swinging/bubbling and respiratory status at agreed intervals.
Escalate sudden large blood loss, loss of swinging, or new respiratory deterioration.

redFlags: Sudden respiratory distress with an absent swing and tracheal deviation — suspect tension pneumothorax or blocked/displaced drain; do not clamp, call for urgent help.
Drain accidentally disconnected or dislodged — cover the site with an occlusive dressing taped on three sides (or per policy) and call for help.
Rapid, large or increasing blood drainage — suspect haemorrhage.

references.label: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline — chest drain management

title: PICC and midline catheter care nursing care plan
summary: Maintenance of peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs) and midline catheters to preserve patency and prevent infection and thrombosis.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Confirm device type, tip position (PICC tip should be central, confirmed before use), insertion date and external length.
Inspect the exit site for erythema, swelling, tenderness or discharge and assess for arm swelling suggesting thrombosis.
Review daily whether the line is still required.

steps.detail: Perform hand hygiene and decontaminate the needle-free connector before every access ('scrub the hub').
Flush using a pulsatile technique and lock per local policy to maintain patency; use a 10 mL or larger syringe to avoid excessive pressure.
Use a securement device and a sterile transparent dressing; change the dressing per policy or if loose/soiled, and measure the external length to detect migration.
Remove the line as soon as it is no longer clinically required.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Document site checks, dressing changes and external length.
Escalate suspected line infection, occlusion or thrombosis.

redFlags: Fever/rigors on flushing with no other source — suspect catheter-related bloodstream infection.
Unilateral arm, neck or facial swelling — suspect catheter-related venous thrombosis.
Resistance to flushing or inability to aspirate — suspect occlusion; do not force.

references.label: CDC Guidelines for the Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections
RCN Standards for infusion therapy

title: Enteral feeding management nursing care plan
summary: Nursing management of enteral tube feeding (NG/gastrostomy) covering tube position confirmation, feed delivery, aspiration prevention and tolerance monitoring.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: For NG feeding, confirm gastric placement before each feed/medication by aspirating and testing on pH indicator paper (pH 5.5 or below).
Assess feed tolerance: nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension, bowel pattern and (where used) gastric residual volumes per local policy.
Assess the tube/stoma site, securement and the patient's nutritional and hydration status.

steps.detail: Sit the patient at 30–45 degrees during and for a period after feeding to reduce the risk of aspiration.
Administer the prescribed feed regimen (continuous or bolus) via pump/gravity per plan; do not exceed prescribed rates.
Flush the tube before and after feeds and medications with water; give medicines in a suitable form to avoid blockage.

steps.step: Care for the tube and site
steps.detail: Secure the tube, rotate gastrostomy tubes if indicated, and provide oral and stoma care.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Record feed delivered, tolerance, fluid balance and weight trend.
Watch for and manage refeeding risk in at-risk/malnourished patients.

redFlags: NEVER feed via an NG tube whose gastric position is unconfirmed — pulmonary misplacement can be fatal (a Never Event).
Coughing, choking or desaturation during feeding — stop and reassess.
In severely malnourished patients, monitor for refeeding syndrome (falling phosphate, potassium, magnesium).

references.label: NICE CG32 — Nutrition support for adults
NHS Improvement / NPSA — Nasogastric tube misplacement

title: Continuous subcutaneous infusion (syringe driver) setup and monitoring care plan
summary: Safe setup and monitoring of a continuous subcutaneous infusion via a syringe pump (driver), commonly in palliative care, to deliver symptom-control medicines over 24 hours.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Confirm the prescription: drug(s), doses, diluent and the duration (commonly over 24 hours), and check compatibility of any combination.
Select a suitable subcutaneous site (e.g. upper arm, abdomen, thigh, upper chest), avoiding broken, oedematous, irradiated or infected skin.
Confirm the correct pump and that staff are trained on the specific device.

steps.detail: Draw up the prescribed drugs and diluent using aseptic technique, check for compatibility and any precipitation, and label the syringe.

steps.step: Set up and start the pump
steps.detail: Load the syringe, prime/connect the infusion set, insert the cannula subcutaneously and secure with a transparent dressing; set the rate per the device and start.
Verify the pump is running at the correct rate, the volume infused is as expected, the battery is adequate and no occlusion alarm is active.
Check the site at least each shift for redness, swelling, leakage or pain and resite if there is a reaction or poor absorption.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Document drugs, rate, volume infused/remaining and site condition at agreed intervals.
Reassess symptom control and escalate inadequate control or adverse effects.

redFlags: Signs of opioid toxicity (increasing drowsiness, reduced respiratory rate, pinpoint pupils, myoclonus) — review the infusion and escalate.
Pump not infusing/occlusion, or a site reaction reducing absorption — symptoms may worsen.
Drug incompatibility (cloudiness/precipitation in the syringe) — do not use.

references.label: NICE NG31 — Care of dying adults in the last days of life
MHRA — Safer use of syringe drivers/infusion pumps guidance

title: Blood glucose monitoring and variable rate insulin (sliding scale) care plan
summary: Capillary blood glucose monitoring and nursing management of a variable rate intravenous insulin infusion (VRIII, 'sliding scale') in hospital inpatients.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Confirm the indication for a VRIII (persistent hyperglycaemia in a patient who is not eating/drinking and cannot use subcutaneous insulin), not for routine diabetic ketoacidosis (which has its own protocol).
Measure capillary blood glucose (CBG) and check baseline electrolytes, particularly potassium.
Confirm the prescribed substrate fluid and any potassium supplementation are running alongside the insulin.

steps.detail: Measure CBG hourly while titrating; if stable, monitoring may be reduced to 2-hourly per protocol. Target inpatient CBG is typically 7–10 mmol/L.
Adjust the soluble-insulin infusion rate (typically 0.5–8 units/hour) according to CBG using the prescribed scale; never stop the insulin abruptly without a plan.
Ensure the prescribed glucose-containing fluid runs concurrently to prevent hypoglycaemia and ketosis, with potassium as prescribed; monitor potassium.
Convert back to the usual subcutaneous regimen with appropriate overlap when the patient is eating and stable.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Document CBG, insulin rate, substrate fluid and potassium results.
Treat hypoglycaemia promptly and review the cause of any deterioration.

redFlags: Hypoglycaemia (CBG below 4 mmol/L) — treat immediately per protocol; do not simply stop the infusion without giving glucose and a plan.
Substrate fluid stopped while insulin continues — risk of hypoglycaemia and ketosis.
Falling potassium during insulin infusion — risk of dangerous hypokalaemia.

references.label: JBDS-IP — The use of variable rate intravenous insulin infusion (VRIII) in adult inpatients

title: Seizure observation and first aid nursing care plan
summary: Immediate first aid and observation during a seizure, protecting the patient from harm, timing the seizure and recognising status epilepticus.

sections.heading: During the seizure
items: Stay with the patient, note the time the seizure starts, and call for help.
Protect from injury: cushion the head, remove nearby hazards and loosen anything tight around the neck.
Do NOT restrain the patient and do NOT put anything in the mouth.
Observe and document the seizure type, duration and features (limb involvement, eyes, incontinence, colour, cyanosis).

steps.detail: Once convulsive movements stop, place the patient on their side (recovery position) to protect the airway.
Assess airway, breathing, circulation; give oxygen if hypoxic and check capillary blood glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia as a cause.
Administer prescribed emergency treatment (e.g. benzodiazepine) for a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or repeated seizures, following the local status epilepticus protocol.
Reassure and orientate the patient during the post-ictal phase, monitor recovery and observations.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Record seizure details, treatment given and time, and recovery.
Review possible precipitants and medication adherence.

redFlags: A convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer, or repeated seizures without recovery between them — treat as status epilepticus, a medical emergency.
Hypoglycaemia as a cause — check and treat blood glucose.
First-ever seizure, focal neurology, head injury, or failure to recover — urgent medical review.

references.label: NICE NG217 — Epilepsies in children, young people and adults

title: Vital signs and NEWS2 escalation nursing care plan
summary: Use of the National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2) to detect deterioration in acutely ill adults and trigger an appropriate, graded clinical response.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Measure and record the six NEWS2 parameters: respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, any supplemental oxygen, temperature, systolic blood pressure, pulse and level of consciousness (ACVPU).
Apply the SpO2 Scale 2 only for patients with a prescribed target range due to hypercapnic respiratory failure risk.
Aggregate the score and identify any single parameter scoring 3 (red score).

steps.detail: Registered nurse assessment; decide whether to increase monitoring frequency or escalate care.

steps.step: Single red score (3 in one parameter)
steps.detail: Urgent review by a clinician competent in assessing acute illness to determine cause and monitoring frequency.
Key threshold for urgent response: urgent review by a clinician/team and a minimum of hourly observations.
Emergency assessment by a critical-care-competent team, continuous monitoring and consideration of transfer to a higher level of care.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Set the observation frequency according to the score and document each set of observations.
Re-score after any intervention and ensure escalation is closed-loop and documented.

redFlags: NEWS2 of 5 or more, or any single parameter scoring 3, indicates potential serious deterioration requiring an urgent clinical response.
NEWS2 of 7 or more requires emergency assessment by a team with critical care competencies.
A rising trend in the score, even if still moderate, is significant — escalate.

references.label: RCP — National Early Warning Score (NEWS) 2

title: Post-fall assessment nursing care plan
summary: Structured nursing assessment and management of an inpatient after a fall, focusing on injury detection, safe handling and prevention of further falls.

sections.heading: Immediate assessment
items: Do not move the patient until injury (especially head, neck and limb fractures) has been assessed; check responsiveness and ABCDE.
Assess for head injury and ask about/observe loss of consciousness, particularly in patients on anticoagulants.
Examine for pain, deformity, bruising or limb shortening/rotation suggesting fracture; record a full set of observations (NEWS2).

steps.detail: Carry out and repeat neurological observations after any fall with head injury or where head injury cannot be excluded, per local protocol.
Escalate for urgent CT head if on anticoagulants with head injury, or if there is reduced consciousness/focal neurology, and arrange limb imaging for suspected fracture.
Provide analgesia, complete an incident report and a post-fall review, and identify the likely cause and contributing factors.
Review medications, mobility, environment and observation level to reduce the risk of recurrence.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Continue observations and neuro obs as indicated and monitor for delayed injury.
Communicate the fall and plan to the team, patient and family.

redFlags: Fall with head injury in a patient on anticoagulants — urgent CT head, as intracranial bleeding can be delayed.
Reduced consciousness, vomiting, focal neurology or seizure after a fall.
Suspected hip/long-bone fracture (pain, shortening, external rotation) — do not mobilise; arrange imaging.

references.label: NICE CG161 — Falls in older people
NICE NG232 — Head injury: assessment and early management

title: Constipation and bowel care nursing care plan
summary: Assessment and management of constipation in hospitalised adults, including recognition of faecal impaction and overflow, and stepwise laxative use.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Take a bowel history: usual pattern, last bowel motion, stool form (e.g. Bristol Stool Chart), straining, and associated symptoms.
Identify contributing factors: immobility, low fibre/fluid intake, opioids and other constipating drugs, dehydration, and ignoring the urge to defaecate.
Assess for faecal impaction with overflow (loose stool/leakage in a constipated patient) and abdominal distension.

steps.detail: Encourage adequate fluid and fibre intake (as appropriate), mobility, and privacy/positioning for toileting.
Use laxatives as prescribed: typically a bulk-forming laxative first with adequate fluids, then add or switch to an osmotic and/or stimulant laxative if needed.
Anticipate and prescribe laxatives prophylactically for patients on opioids; avoid bulk-forming laxatives alone in opioid-induced constipation.
For faecal impaction, escalate for an appropriate regimen (e.g. high-dose oral macrogol, or rectal measures such as suppositories/enemas) per guideline and local policy.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Record bowel movements on a stool chart and evaluate response.
Review and rationalise constipating medications.

redFlags: New, persistent change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding, weight loss or anaemia — exclude serious bowel pathology.
Severe abdominal pain, distension, vomiting and absolute constipation — suspect bowel obstruction.
Overflow diarrhoea/incontinence in a constipated patient — suspect faecal impaction, not simple diarrhoea.

references.label: NICE CKS — Constipation

title: Palliative mouth and pressure area comfort care plan
summary: Comfort-focused nursing care of the mouth and pressure areas for patients in the last days of life, prioritising dignity and symptom relief.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Assess the mouth for dryness, coating, candidiasis, ulcers and discomfort, and the lips for cracking.
Assess skin and pressure areas, balancing repositioning needs against comfort in the dying patient.
Assess the person's ability to take oral fluids and their wishes/those of the family.

steps.detail: Offer regular gentle mouth care: moisten the mouth and lips, clean as tolerated, and use saliva substitutes/lip balm; treat oral thrush if present.
Offer sips of fluid and ice chips as tolerated; make individualised, shared decisions about clinically assisted hydration.
Provide a pressure-redistributing surface and reposition gently and individually, prioritising comfort and avoiding distressing the patient.
Teach willing family members to give mouth care and explain the comfort focus of care.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
items: Reassess comfort frequently and adjust the frequency of care to the individual.
Document mouth and skin care and any distressing symptoms for escalation.

redFlags: Distressing oral pain, candidiasis or bleeding — treat and escalate to palliative care.
New or worsening pressure damage causing pain or distress.

references.label: NICE NG31 — Care of dying adults in the last days of life

title: Urethral catheterisation troubleshooting
summary: Systematic troubleshooting of difficult or failed urethral catheterisation in adults, including non-drainage, resistance and balloon problems.

sections.heading: Difficult insertion (resistance)
items: In males, resistance commonly occurs at the external sphincter or prostate; apply gentle steady traction with the penis vertical and ask the patient to relax/breathe; instil adequate anaesthetic lubricant and allow it to work.
Never force the catheter; if resistance persists or there is a stricture/false passage suspicion, stop and seek urology advice.
Consider a different catheter size; do not repeatedly attempt traumatic passage.

steps.detail: If no urine drains, do NOT inflate the balloon; advance the catheter further (to the hilt in males) — the tip may not yet be in the bladder, especially in a dry/empty bladder.
Flush gently with sterile saline to confirm patency and check tubing is not kinked; lubricant in the eyes can occlude flow initially.
Pain on attempted balloon inflation suggests the balloon is in the urethra — deflate and reassess; do not inflate against resistance.

If the balloon will not deflate, leave the syringe attached to allow passive deflation, try a different syringe, and check the valve; follow local policy and seek senior/urology help — never cut the catheter or burst the balloon blindly.

redFlags: Frank haematuria, severe pain or inability to pass the catheter — stop and seek urology advice (possible false passage or stricture).
Always replace a retracted foreskin after the procedure to prevent paraphimosis.
Pain on balloon inflation — the balloon may be in the urethra; deflate immediately.

references.label: NICE QS61 — Infection prevention and control: urinary catheters
BAUS — Urethral catheterisation guidance

title: Suprapubic catheter care and change
summary: Care and routine change of an established suprapubic catheter, including stoma site care and safe technique.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm the catheter is well established (first change of a suprapubic catheter should be performed by a competent practitioner, not before the tract has matured — typically several weeks after insertion).
Gather a sterile catheter pack, an appropriate suprapubic catheter, lubricant, a sterile water-filled syringe and a drainage system.
Perform hand hygiene and use aseptic non-touch technique; ensure privacy.

steps.detail: Inspect the suprapubic stoma for infection, overgranulation or encrustation and clean per policy.
Deflate the balloon fully and gently withdraw the catheter along the tract; note the angle/length for reinsertion.
Lubricate and insert the new catheter through the tract until urine flows; only then inflate the balloon with sterile water to the stated volume.
Connect to a closed drainage system, secure the catheter and document the change, catheter type and any difficulty.

redFlags: Inability to reinsert after removal — the tract can close quickly; keep it patent and seek urgent help to avoid losing the tract.
No urine drainage or pain on balloon inflation — stop; do not inflate in a false passage.
Signs of infection at the site or systemic sepsis.

references.label: BAUS — Suprapubic catheter guidance
NICE QS61 — Infection prevention and control: urinary catheters

title: Central venous catheter insertion
summary: Ultrasound-guided insertion of a central venous catheter (typically internal jugular) using full aseptic technique and the Seldinger method.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm indication and consent; check coagulation and platelets and correct significant abnormalities where feasible.
Use maximal sterile barrier precautions (cap, mask, sterile gown and gloves, large sterile drape) and chlorhexidine skin antisepsis.
Use real-time ultrasound guidance for internal jugular access; identify the vein (compressible, non-pulsatile) and surrounding structures.

steps.detail: Under ultrasound, insert the introducer needle into the vein and confirm dark, non-pulsatile venous blood return.
Thread the guidewire through the needle (monitor for arrhythmias from the wire), remove the needle leaving the wire in place, and never let go of the wire.
Make a small skin nick, pass the dilator over the wire, then railroad the catheter over the wire; remove the wire and aspirate/flush each lumen to confirm venous placement.
Secure the catheter, apply a sterile dressing, and confirm tip position and exclude pneumothorax with a chest X-ray before use of the central lumen.

redFlags: Bright red pulsatile blood or a pressure-transduced arterial trace — arterial puncture; do not dilate; remove and apply pressure or seek vascular/senior help.
New breathlessness, hypoxia or chest pain after insertion — suspect pneumothorax.
Air embolism risk: position head-down for insertion/removal of upper-body lines and never leave the hub open to air.

references.label: NICE TA49 — Guidance on the use of ultrasound locating devices for placing central venous catheters
CDC Guidelines for the Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections

title: Arterial line (radial) insertion
summary: Insertion of a radial arterial catheter for continuous blood pressure monitoring and repeated arterial sampling.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm indication and consent; assess collateral circulation (e.g. modified Allen's test) and choose the non-dominant wrist where possible.
Use aseptic technique with chlorhexidine skin antisepsis; prepare a primed, zeroed transducer set with pressurised flush.
Position the wrist in slight dorsiflexion and palpate (or ultrasound-locate) the radial artery.

steps.detail: Infiltrate local anaesthetic if appropriate; insert the cannula at a shallow angle toward the palpated pulse until pulsatile arterial flashback is seen.
Lower the angle and advance the catheter into the artery (directly or over a guidewire), confirming pulsatile flow.
Connect to the transducer system, flush, and zero the transducer at the phlebostatic axis to obtain an accurate arterial waveform and pressure.
Secure the cannula, apply a sterile dressing and clearly label the line as ARTERIAL to prevent accidental drug administration.

redFlags: NEVER inject medication into an arterial line — intra-arterial drug injection can cause limb-threatening ischaemia; clearly label the line.
Distal pallor, pain, paraesthesia or absent pulse — suspect arterial occlusion/ischaemia; remove the line.
Accidental disconnection can cause rapid significant blood loss — keep connections visible and secure.

references.label: NHS England / NHSI — Patient Safety Alert on arterial line misconnection/labelling

title: Ascitic tap and paracentesis
summary: Diagnostic ascitic tap and therapeutic paracentesis (drainage) of ascites, with ascitic fluid analysis to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm indication and consent; perform a diagnostic tap in any patient with new ascites or decompensation to look for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP).
Check coagulation; significant coagulopathy is a relative contraindication — discuss with seniors.
Use ultrasound to mark/guide the site (commonly the left lower quadrant, lateral to the rectus, avoiding scars, vessels and organs); empty the bladder.

steps.detail: Clean with antiseptic, drape, and infiltrate local anaesthetic for therapeutic drainage; use aseptic technique.
Insert the needle/cannula (a 'Z-track' technique reduces leakage) into the ascites and aspirate fluid; send for cell count/neutrophils, culture, albumin and protein.

For large-volume paracentesis, connect a drainage catheter and drain to the planned volume; give intravenous albumin replacement as indicated for large-volume drainage to prevent circulatory dysfunction.
Remove the catheter, apply a dressing and monitor the site for leakage and the patient for haemodynamic change.

redFlags: Ascitic neutrophil count of 250 cells/mm3 or more indicates spontaneous bacterial peritonitis — start antibiotics urgently.
Large-volume paracentesis without albumin replacement can precipitate post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction and renal impairment.
Persistent bleeding, bowel perforation (peritonism) or haemodynamic instability.

references.label: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on decompensated cirrhosis (ascites/SBP)

title: Knee joint aspiration (arthrocentesis)
summary: Aspiration of synovial fluid from the knee for diagnosis (especially to exclude septic arthritis) and symptom relief, using aseptic technique.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm indication and consent; the key urgent indication is suspected septic arthritis (hot, swollen, painful joint) — aspirate before antibiotics where possible.
Do NOT aspirate through overlying cellulitis or infected skin; check for coagulopathy.
Use strict aseptic technique with skin antisepsis; position the knee slightly flexed and identify landmarks (e.g. superolateral or medial patellar approach).

steps.detail: Clean the skin, drape, and infiltrate local anaesthetic to skin and deeper tissues if needed.
Insert the needle at the chosen landmark into the joint space and aspirate synovial fluid; if draining an effusion, withdraw as much as needed for relief.
Send fluid for urgent Gram stain and culture, cell count, and polarised-light microscopy for crystals (gout/pseudogout).
Withdraw the needle, apply pressure and a dressing, and document the appearance and volume of fluid.

redFlags: Turbid/purulent aspirate, a markedly raised synovial white cell count, or organisms on Gram stain — treat as septic arthritis, a joint- and limb-threatening emergency.
A hot swollen joint with fever must be assumed septic until proven otherwise — do not delay aspiration/escalation.
Do not aspirate through cellulitis (risk of seeding the joint).

references.label: BSR — Guideline for the management of hot swollen joint / septic arthritis

title: Nasojejunal vs nasogastric tube placement
summary: Considerations and placement of post-pyloric nasojejunal (NJ) feeding compared with nasogastric (NG) feeding, including position confirmation.

sections.heading: Choosing NG vs NJ
items: NG feeding delivers feed to the stomach and is first-line for most patients needing short-term enteral nutrition.
NJ (post-pyloric) feeding is used when gastric feeding fails or is unsafe — e.g. delayed gastric emptying, severe gastro-oesophageal reflux, high aspiration risk, or some pancreatitis cases.
NJ tubes are placed beyond the pylorus into the jejunum, often endoscopically, fluoroscopically or with electromagnetic/bedside placement systems.

steps.detail: Insert per the chosen method; NG by the standard nasogastric technique, NJ by a competent operator using imaging or a guided placement system to pass the pylorus.
For NG tubes, confirm gastric placement before use by aspirate pH of 5.5 or below; if not obtained/reliable, use chest X-ray interpreted by a competent practitioner.
Post-pyloric NJ position is confirmed radiologically (aspirate pH is unreliable beyond the stomach as jejunal contents are more alkaline).
Secure the tube, record the external length and confirmation method, and recheck length before each use.

redFlags: NEVER feed via any nasoenteral tube whose position is unconfirmed — pulmonary misplacement can be fatal (a Never Event).
Do not rely on aspirate pH to confirm a post-pyloric (NJ) tube; use radiological confirmation.
Respiratory distress or coughing during insertion — withdraw immediately (possible tracheal placement).

references.label: NHS Improvement / NPSA — Nasogastric tube misplacement
NICE CG32 — Nutrition support for adults

title: Defibrillation and synchronised cardioversion
summary: Delivery of an asynchronous defibrillation shock for shockable cardiac arrest rhythms and a synchronised DC cardioversion for unstable tachyarrhythmias with a pulse.

steps.detail: During CPR, briefly pause to assess the rhythm; defibrillate only ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia.
Select energy (e.g. 150 J biphasic per local device, escalating if needed), keep compressions going while charging, then ensure everyone is clear and oxygen is removed from the field.

steps.step: Deliver the shock and resume CPR
steps.detail: Deliver the shock and immediately resume chest compressions for 2 minutes before reassessing the rhythm.

sections.heading: Synchronised cardioversion (unstable tachycardia WITH a pulse)

steps.detail: Cardiovert an unstable tachyarrhythmia (shock, syncope, ischaemia, heart failure) under sedation/anaesthesia; engage SYNC mode so the shock is timed to the R wave to avoid the T wave.
For broad-complex tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, start at 120–150 J biphasic and escalate if needed; for atrial flutter/regular narrow-complex SVT start lower (around 70–120 J biphasic).
Re-check the rhythm after each shock and re-engage SYNC before each subsequent synchronised shock.

redFlags: NEVER deliver an unsynchronised shock to a conscious patient with a pulse — an unsynchronised shock on the T wave can induce VF.
Ensure all team members and oxygen are clear before discharging the defibrillator.
Remove transdermal patches and avoid pads over an implanted device generator.

references.label: Resuscitation Council UK — Advanced Life Support / Tachycardia guidance

title: Transcutaneous (external) cardiac pacing
summary: Emergency external pacing for haemodynamically unstable bradycardia unresponsive to drugs, as a bridge to transvenous pacing.

sections.heading: Indication and preparation
items: Indicated for unstable bradycardia (with shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia or heart failure) not responding to atropine, or as standby for high-risk AV block.
Apply the pacing pads (anterior-posterior or per device) and attach ECG monitoring; explain to the patient and provide analgesia/sedation as it is painful.
Ensure resuscitation equipment is available.

steps.detail: Select pacing mode and set a rate (e.g. around 60–80 bpm), usually in demand mode.
Gradually increase the current (mA) until electrical capture is seen (a pacing spike followed by a broad QRS) and confirm mechanical capture by a palpable pulse matching the paced rate.
Set the output slightly above the threshold for reliable capture and monitor continuously.
Use as a bridge and arrange urgent transvenous pacing or cardiology input.

redFlags: Do not assume pacing is effective from the monitor alone — always confirm mechanical capture by a palpable pulse, as electrical spikes can occur without output (failure to capture).
External pacing is painful — provide analgesia/sedation in the conscious patient.
Persistent instability despite pacing — escalate urgently for transvenous pacing.

references.label: Resuscitation Council UK — Peri-arrest arrhythmias / Bradycardia algorithm

title: Manual removal of faeces
summary: Digital removal of impacted stool from the rectum when other measures have failed, performed by a competent practitioner with monitoring for vagal effects.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm the indication (faecal impaction unresponsive to oral/rectal laxatives) and obtain consent; ensure it is performed only by a trained, competent practitioner.
Check for contraindications/cautions: recent rectal/anal surgery, active inflammatory bowel disease, recent radiotherapy, spinal injury risk of autonomic dysreflexia, and bleeding tendency.
Record baseline pulse and ensure privacy and dignity; gather gloves, lubricant and protective sheeting.

steps.detail: Position the patient in the left lateral position with knees flexed; perform a gentle digital rectal examination first.
Using a well-lubricated gloved finger, gently break up and remove small amounts of stool at a time; never use force or hooking that could damage the mucosa.
Observe the patient throughout and stop if there is bradycardia, a drop in pulse/BP, distress, bleeding or severe pain (vagal stimulation/autonomic dysreflexia risk).
Provide hygiene afterwards, document the amount/consistency removed and the patient's response, and review the bowel care plan.

redFlags: Bradycardia, hypotension or collapse during the procedure — stop immediately (vagal stimulation).
In patients with spinal cord injury above T6, watch for autonomic dysreflexia (severe hypertension, headache) — stop and treat as an emergency.
Rectal bleeding, severe pain or signs of perforation.

references.label: RCN — Management of lower bowel dysfunction / digital rectal procedures guidance

title: Wound packing (cavity wound)
summary: Packing of a cavity or undermined wound to manage exudate and promote healing from the base, using aseptic non-touch technique.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Assess the wound dimensions, depth, undermining/tunnelling, tissue type, exudate and signs of infection.
Select an appropriate packing material matched to the exudate and cavity; gather a sterile dressing pack and irrigation fluid.
Perform hand hygiene and use aseptic non-touch technique (ANTT).

steps.detail: Irrigate/cleanse the cavity per policy and assess the wound bed and edges.
Gently pack the material to fill the cavity in contact with the wound base WITHOUT over-packing — over-tight packing causes pressure damage and impairs healing.
Ensure the entire pack is in one retrievable piece (or count/record strips) and that none is left behind; document the amount used.
Cover with an appropriate secondary dressing and document wound measurements and the packing used for the next change.

redFlags: Retained packing material is a risk — always record and remove the full amount used at the next change.
Spreading cellulitis, increasing pain, malodour or systemic sepsis — treat infection.
A deep wound probing to bone — consider osteomyelitis and refer.

references.label: NICE — Chronic wounds: advanced wound dressings (ESMPB2)

title: Plaster cast and backslab application
summary: Application of a plaster of Paris or synthetic backslab/cast to immobilise a fracture or soft-tissue injury, with safe technique and complication awareness.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm the indication, injury and any reduction performed; assess and document distal neurovascular status before application.
In acute injury, apply a backslab (non-circumferential) rather than a complete cast to allow for swelling.
Gather stockinette, padding, casting material, warm (not hot) water and protect the patient's skin and clothing.

steps.detail: Apply stockinette and an even layer of padding, with extra padding over bony prominences, before the casting material.
Apply the wetted casting material in the position of immobilisation, moulding gently; avoid indentations from fingertips that can cause pressure sores.
Maintain the required position until the material sets; avoid weight-bearing/handling until fully hardened.
Recheck distal neurovascular status, give written cast-care and warning advice (elevation, what to watch for), and arrange follow-up.

redFlags: A cast that is too tight or unrelenting pain, paraesthesia, pallor or loss of distal pulses — suspect compartment syndrome or vascular compromise; split/remove the cast and escalate urgently.
Pain under the cast, a burning sensation or a foul smell — possible pressure sore or infection beneath the cast.
Never apply a complete circumferential cast over an acutely swelling injury.

references.label: BOAST (British Orthopaedic Association Standards for Trauma) — casting/plaster standards

title: Reduction of common joint dislocations (overview)
summary: General principles for the closed reduction of common dislocations (e.g. shoulder, finger, patella), emphasising neurovascular assessment, analgesia and post-reduction checks.

sections.heading: Assessment before reduction
items: Assess and document distal neurovascular status BEFORE attempting reduction; for the shoulder, specifically check axillary nerve sensation over the deltoid (regimental badge area).
Obtain pre-reduction imaging where appropriate to confirm the dislocation and exclude fracture (fracture-dislocations may need orthopaedic input).
Provide adequate analgesia and/or procedural sedation per protocol.

steps.detail: Use an appropriate recognised reduction technique for the joint with slow, sustained, gentle traction and patient relaxation rather than sudden force.
Confirm successful reduction clinically (restored contour, range, reduced pain) and with post-reduction imaging where indicated.
Re-check and document distal neurovascular status AFTER reduction — a new deficit must be acted on.
Immobilise appropriately (e.g. sling, splint) and arrange orthopaedic follow-up; refer fracture-dislocations and failed/irreducible cases.

redFlags: New or worsening neurovascular deficit after reduction — urgent orthopaedic assessment.
Irreducible dislocation, fracture-dislocation, or open injury — do not persist; refer to orthopaedics.
Suspected hip dislocation/prosthetic dislocation — needs imaging and specialist reduction.

references.label: BOAST (British Orthopaedic Association Standards for Trauma)

title: Hand hygiene technique (handwashing and hand rub steps)
summary: Correct technique for hand hygiene using alcohol-based handrub or soap and water, following the WHO step-by-step method to ensure all surfaces of the hands are covered.

sections.heading: Choosing the method
items: Use alcohol-based handrub as the preferred routine method when hands are not visibly soiled.

Wash with soap and water when hands are visibly dirty or soiled, after using the toilet, and when caring for patients with spore-forming organisms (e.g. Clostridioides difficile, where alcohol is not sporicidal).
Ensure 'bare below the elbows', remove rings/wrist jewellery, keep nails short and avoid artificial nails.

steps.detail: Apply handrub to a cupped hand (or wet hands and apply soap); rub palm to palm.
Rub right palm over left dorsum with interlaced fingers and vice versa; then palm to palm with fingers interlaced.
Rub backs of fingers to opposing palms with fingers interlocked; rotationally rub each clasped thumb; then rotationally rub fingertips/nails in the opposite palm.
Handrub: rub until dry (about 20–30 seconds). Handwash: rinse, dry thoroughly with a single-use towel (about 40–60 seconds total) and use the towel to turn off the tap.

redFlags: Alcohol handrub is NOT effective against Clostridioides difficile or norovirus — use soap and water for these.
Visibly soiled hands must be washed with soap and water, not just handrubbed.

references.label: WHO Guidelines on Hand Hygiene in Health Care

title: Aseptic non-touch technique (ANTT)
summary: Standardised aseptic technique framework based on identifying and protecting key-parts and key-sites to prevent introduction of microorganisms during invasive procedures.

sections.heading: Core concepts
items: A KEY-PART is any sterile part of the equipment that, if contaminated, could introduce infection (e.g. needle hub, syringe tip, exposed needle, dressing in contact with the wound).
A KEY-SITE is the site on the patient that is vulnerable to infection (e.g. the insertion point/open wound).
Asepsis is achieved by protecting key-parts and key-sites throughout, combining hand hygiene, PPE, aseptic field management, non-touch technique and sterile supplies.

steps.detail: Assess the procedure to choose Standard-ANTT (general aseptic field with micro critical fields for individual key-parts) or Surgical-ANTT (critical aseptic field/sterile drapes) for more complex/longer procedures.
Perform hand hygiene, put on appropriate PPE/gloves, and prepare a clean/sterile aseptic field; decontaminate any reusable equipment.
Identify, then protect, all key-parts and key-sites; use a non-touch technique so key-parts are never touched directly even when wearing gloves.
Carry out the procedure maintaining asepsis, dispose of waste/sharps safely and perform hand hygiene afterwards.

redFlags: Touching a key-part or key-site (even with gloves on) breaks asepsis — replace the contaminated item and restart that step.
Inadequate hand hygiene before the procedure undermines the whole technique.

references.label: The ANTT Clinical Practice Framework (Association for Safe Aseptic Practice)
NICE QS61 / epic3 — aseptic technique for invasive devices

title: Peripheral cannula insertion and maintenance bundle
summary: Care bundle of evidence-based elements applied at insertion and during maintenance of a peripheral venous cannula to prevent infection and phlebitis.

sections.heading: Insertion bundle
items: Insert only when clinically necessary and document the date, time and site.
Perform hand hygiene and use aseptic non-touch technique with single-use gloves.
Decontaminate the skin with 2% chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% alcohol and allow it to dry fully; do not re-palpate the cleaned site.
Use a sterile, transparent semi-permeable dressing that allows inspection of the site.

steps.detail: Assess the site at least daily using a Visual Infusion Phlebitis (VIP) score for redness, pain, swelling or discharge.
Decontaminate the needle-free connector/port before every access and allow it to dry.
Review the ongoing need for the cannula each day and remove it as soon as it is no longer required, or immediately if signs of phlebitis/infection appear.
Replace the dressing if it becomes loose, wet or soiled, maintaining asepsis.

redFlags: Phlebitis (pain, erythema, palpable cord) or signs of infection at the site — remove the cannula immediately.
Spreading erythema, pus or systemic sepsis — escalate and consider catheter-related infection.

references.label: epic3 / NICE CG139 — Healthcare-associated infections: intravascular devices
RCN Standards for infusion therapy

title: Blood culture collection and contamination prevention
summary: Aseptic technique for collecting blood cultures to maximise diagnostic yield and minimise contamination, which causes false positives and unnecessary antibiotics.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Collect cultures ideally before starting antibiotics and when clinically indicated (e.g. suspected sepsis), taking an adequate blood volume per bottle.
Perform hand hygiene and use aseptic non-touch technique; obtain from a fresh venepuncture rather than an existing catheter where possible (line cultures have higher contamination).
Gather chlorhexidine/alcohol skin antiseptic, sterile gloves and the culture bottles.

steps.detail: Clean the venepuncture site with 2% chlorhexidine in alcohol and allow it to dry completely; do NOT re-palpate the cleaned site with a non-sterile finger.
Decontaminate the tops of the culture bottles with an alcohol/antiseptic wipe and allow to dry before inoculation.
Collect the recommended blood volume and inoculate the bottles (follow the recommended order and fill volume); avoid touching the needle or bottle septum.
Label the bottles and send promptly to the laboratory.

redFlags: Skin/needle contamination produces false-positive cultures, leading to unnecessary antibiotics and prolonged stays.
In suspected sepsis, do not delay antibiotics solely to obtain cultures beyond the recommended window.

references.label: Public Health England / UKHSA — SMI B37: Investigation of blood cultures (taking blood cultures)

title: Multidrug-resistant organism (MRSA/CRE) precautions
summary: Infection prevention measures for patients colonised or infected with multidrug-resistant organisms such as MRSA and carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE/CPE).

sections.heading: Identification and assessment
items: Screen at-risk patients on admission per local policy (e.g. MRSA screening; CRE/CPE screening for previous carriers or those with relevant healthcare contact abroad).
Flag known carriers and communicate status on transfer.
Identify the organism and the body sites colonised/infected.

steps.detail: Place the patient in a single room (with en-suite if possible) for contact precautions; cohort with dedicated staff/equipment if single rooms are limited.
Perform hand hygiene and wear gloves and aprons/gowns for contact; use dedicated or single-use equipment and decontaminate shared equipment between patients.
Increase the frequency and thoroughness of cleaning/disinfection of the room and high-touch surfaces.
Carry out MRSA decolonisation regimens where indicated; treat infection per microbiology advice and antimicrobial stewardship.

redFlags: CRE/CPE carriers are a major cross-transmission risk with very limited treatment options — strict contact precautions and prompt isolation are essential.
Breaches in hand hygiene and environmental cleaning drive outbreaks of resistant organisms.

references.label: CDC — Management of Multidrug-Resistant Organisms in Healthcare Settings
PHE/UKHSA — Acute trust toolkit for the early detection, management and control of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales

title: Needlestick and sharps injury management
summary: Immediate first aid and reporting after a needlestick/sharps or blood/body-fluid exposure, including risk assessment and post-exposure prophylaxis where indicated.

sections.heading: Immediate first aid
items: Encourage the wound to bleed gently — do NOT suck it.
Wash the wound with running water and soap; do not scrub.
For mucous membrane/eye splashes, irrigate copiously with water or saline; remove contact lenses and continue irrigation.
Do not apply caustic agents (e.g. bleach) to the wound.

steps.detail: Report the exposure straight away to the line manager/occupational health or emergency department per local policy; complete an incident report.
A trained assessor evaluates the risk based on the device, depth of injury, body fluid involved and the source patient's blood-borne virus status (with consent for source testing).
For significant HIV exposure, start PEP as soon as possible — ideally within 1 hour and no later than 72 hours; assess hepatitis B status/booster and hepatitis C follow-up.
Take baseline bloods as indicated and arrange follow-up serology per protocol.

redFlags: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is time-critical — start as soon as possible (within hours), do not wait for source results.
High-risk source (known HIV/hepatitis, deep injury, hollow-bore blood-filled needle) — escalate urgently to occupational health/emergency care.

references.label: CDC — Management of Occupational Blood Exposures / PEP guidance
UK Health and Safety (Sharps Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations / UKHSA exposure guidance

title: Safe injection practices
summary: Practices to prevent transmission of infection during injections and infusions, including single-use of needles/syringes and safe handling of medication vials.

sections.heading: Core principles
items: Use a sterile, single-use needle and syringe for each injection and for each patient.
Never re-use a needle or syringe to access a medication vial or solution that will be used for more than one patient.
Prepare injections using aseptic technique in a clean, dedicated area.
Use single-dose vials where possible and discard any remainder; do not combine leftover contents.

steps.detail: Perform hand hygiene and use aseptic non-touch technique when preparing and giving injections.
Wipe the vial septum/access port with alcohol and allow it to dry before inserting a sterile device.
If a multi-dose vial must be used, dedicate it to a single patient where possible, use a new sterile needle/syringe each access, and store/discard per policy and expiry.
Dispose of needles and syringes into a sharps container at the point of use without recapping.

redFlags: Re-using needles/syringes or accessing shared vials with used equipment has caused outbreaks of hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV — never do this.
A used syringe is contaminated even if the needle is changed — discard the whole device.

references.label: WHO Best Practices for Injections and Related Procedures Toolkit
CDC — Injection Safety / One & Only Campaign

title: Blood and body fluid spill decontamination
summary: Safe management of blood and body-fluid spillages, including PPE, containment and disinfection, to reduce the risk of blood-borne virus transmission.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Obtain a spill kit and appropriate PPE (gloves, apron; eye/face protection if splashing is likely).
Cordon off the area to prevent contact by others.
Identify the type/volume of spill and the surface involved.

steps.detail: Cover/contain the spill with absorbent material (e.g. paper towels or the granules in the spill kit) to soak up the bulk of the fluid.

Apply a chlorine-releasing disinfectant at the recommended concentration for the surface (commonly around 10,000 ppm available chlorine for blood spills) and leave for the required contact time; do not use chlorine directly on urine spills (risk of toxic chlorine gas) — soak up urine first.
Remove the absorbed material into clinical waste, then clean the area with detergent and water and allow to dry.
Dispose of waste and PPE as clinical/contaminated waste and perform hand hygiene.

redFlags: Do not pour chlorine-releasing agents directly onto urine spills — this can release toxic chlorine gas; absorb the urine first.
Any associated sharps injury or mucosal exposure during clean-up must be managed as an occupational exposure.

references.label: UKHSA / PHE — Guidance on the management of blood and body fluid spillages

title: Paediatric maintenance IV fluids (Holliday-Segar / 4-2-1 rule)
summary: Calculation of routine maintenance intravenous fluid requirements in children using the Holliday-Segar method, with the 4-2-1 rule for hourly rates and isotonic fluid choice.

sections.heading: Daily volume (Holliday-Segar)
items: First 10 kg of body weight: 100 mL/kg/day.
Second 10 kg (11–20 kg): add 50 mL/kg/day.
Each kg above 20 kg: add 20 mL/kg/day.
Example: a 22 kg child = (10 x 100) + (10 x 50) + (2 x 20) = 1540 mL/day.

steps.detail: 4 mL/kg/hour for the first 10 kg, plus 2 mL/kg/hour for the second 10 kg, plus 1 mL/kg/hour for each kg above 20 kg. Example: a 22 kg child = (4 x 10) + (2 x 10) + (1 x 2) = 62 mL/hour.

Use an isotonic solution (e.g. 0.9% sodium chloride, with glucose as required) for maintenance in children to reduce the risk of hospital-acquired hyponatraemia; avoid hypotonic fluids for routine maintenance.
Maintenance volumes do not include correction of dehydration or ongoing abnormal losses — assess and add these separately.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: Monitor weight, fluid balance, clinical hydration and serum electrolytes (especially sodium) at least daily on IV fluids.
Reassess the prescription regularly and stop IV fluids once oral intake is adequate.

redFlags: Hypotonic maintenance fluids in children can cause acute, potentially fatal hyponatraemia and cerebral oedema — use isotonic fluids and monitor sodium.
Acute drop in sodium with headache, vomiting, irritability or seizures — suspect hyponatraemic encephalopathy.

references.label: NICE NG29 — Intravenous fluid therapy in children and young people in hospital
Holliday MA, Segar WE. The maintenance need for water in parenteral fluid therapy. Pediatrics 1957

title: Burns fluid resuscitation (Parkland formula)
summary: Estimation and delivery of fluid resuscitation in significant burns using the Parkland formula, titrated to urine output, with crystalloid (Hartmann's/Ringer's lactate).

sections.heading: Calculation (Parkland formula)
items: Total fluid in the first 24 hours = 4 mL x body weight (kg) x % total body surface area (TBSA) burned, using a crystalloid such as Hartmann's solution (Ringer's lactate).
Give HALF of the calculated volume in the first 8 hours and the remaining half over the next 16 hours.
Crucially, the first 8 hours runs from the TIME OF THE BURN, not the time of assessment — if presentation is delayed, give the first half over the remaining time.
Example: an 80 kg adult with 16% TBSA burn = 4 x 80 x 16 = 5120 mL in 24 hours (2560 mL in the first 8 hours from injury).

steps.detail: Estimate %TBSA (e.g. Wallace Rule of Nines or a Lund and Browder chart); count partial- and full-thickness burns, not simple erythema.
The formula is a starting estimate only — titrate the rate to a target urine output of approximately 0.5–1 mL/kg/hour in adults (higher targets in children/electrical burns) and adjust accordingly.
Monitor for under- and over-resuscitation ('fluid creep'); excessive fluid causes oedema, compartment syndromes and respiratory compromise.

redFlags: Inadequate resuscitation risks shock and acute kidney injury; over-resuscitation risks compartment syndrome and pulmonary oedema — titrate to urine output, not the formula alone.
Circumferential full-thickness burns to limbs or chest may need escharotomy — watch for distal ischaemia or impaired ventilation.
Suspected inhalation injury — secure the airway early.

references.label: Parkland Formula — StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf)

title: Hypertonic saline for symptomatic hyponatraemia
summary: Use of 3% hypertonic saline to treat severely symptomatic hyponatraemia, with strict limits on the rate of sodium correction to avoid osmotic demyelination.

sections.heading: Indication and approach
items: Reserve 3% hypertonic saline for SEVERE symptomatic hyponatraemia (e.g. seizures, marked obtundation, coma) — a hyponatraemic encephalopathy emergency.

European guidance recommends a bolus approach: 150 mL of 3% hypertonic saline over about 20 minutes, which can be repeated, aiming to raise serum sodium by about 4–6 mmol/L to relieve life-threatening symptoms.
Manage in a monitored setting with senior/critical-care input.

steps.detail: Do NOT raise serum sodium by more than 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours (many use an 8–10 mmol/L limit; lower in high-risk patients) to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome.

steps.step: Aim for an initial small rise
steps.detail: Target a prompt rise of only about 4–6 mmol/L to abolish severe symptoms, then stop the rapid correction.
Recheck serum sodium frequently (e.g. every 2–4 hours during active treatment) so as not to overcorrect; reassess before repeating a bolus.
If sodium rises too fast/too far, stop hypertonic saline and seek expert advice on re-lowering (e.g. with dextrose +/- desmopressin) per protocol.

redFlags: Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis) — a devastating, often delayed and irreversible neurological injury.
Never use hypertonic saline without close monitoring and a clear correction limit.
Acute hyponatraemia with seizures/coma is an emergency requiring immediate treatment.

references.label: European clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia (ERA-EDTA/ESE/ESICM)

title: Potassium infusion rate and monitoring limits
summary: Safe intravenous potassium replacement, including maximum peripheral infusion rates, concentration limits and monitoring requirements to prevent fatal hyperkalaemia.

sections.heading: Safe limits
items: Use ready-made pre-mixed potassium solutions wherever possible; never give a rapid IV bolus or undiluted potassium — this can cause fatal cardiac arrest.
Peripheral line: typical maximum concentration is 40 mmol/L and a maximum rate of 10 mmol/hour.
Higher concentrations/rates (e.g. >10 mmol/hour) require a central line, an infusion pump and continuous cardiac (ECG) monitoring in a high-dependency setting.
Avoid exceeding usual total daily replacement without specialist review.

steps.detail: Administer via a volumetric infusion pump; never as a push/bolus.

steps.step: Match the setting to the rate
steps.detail: Use peripheral administration only within the safe concentration/rate limits; rates above 10 mmol/hour need central access and continuous cardiac monitoring.

steps.step: Recheck potassium and protect the heart
steps.detail: Recheck serum potassium during and after replacement, monitor renal function, and watch the ECG; faster regimens mandate continuous monitoring.
Watch peripheral sites for pain/phlebitis (potassium is irritant) and slow or resite as needed.

redFlags: Rapid or concentrated IV potassium can cause fatal hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest — never bolus and always control the rate.
Beware potassium replacement in renal impairment or oliguria — risk of dangerous hyperkalaemia.
ECG changes (peaked T waves, widened QRS) during infusion — stop and treat as an emergency.

references.label: NPSA Patient Safety Alert 01 — Potassium chloride concentrate solutions (safe handling)
Medinfo / hospital IV monograph — Potassium chloride intravenous infusion for adults

title: Magnesium replacement protocol
summary: Intravenous magnesium sulfate replacement for hypomagnesaemia, including dosing for severe/symptomatic deficiency and rate limits, with monitoring.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Confirm hypomagnesaemia and consider causes (GI/renal losses, alcohol, drugs such as PPIs and diuretics, refeeding).
Hypomagnesaemia commonly coexists with and causes refractory hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia — replace magnesium to correct these.
Assess for symptoms (tremor, tetany, seizures, arrhythmias) and check renal function (reduce dose/monitor closely in renal impairment).

steps.detail: Give IV magnesium sulfate per local protocol — e.g. a common regimen is 20 mmol (about 5 g) of magnesium sulfate diluted in 100 mL or more of 0.9% sodium chloride or 5% glucose, infused over at least a few hours (commonly not exceeding around 8 mmol/hour).
In peri-arrest arrhythmia or eclampsia, magnesium is given more rapidly per the specific emergency protocol (e.g. 2 g over several minutes); follow the relevant guideline.
Do not infuse too quickly outside emergency protocols — rapid administration risks hypotension, flushing and, at high levels, respiratory depression and cardiac toxicity.
Correct coexisting potassium and calcium deficits, as low magnesium impairs their correction.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: Recheck serum magnesium (and potassium/calcium) after replacement; deficits may need repeated dosing over several days.
Monitor blood pressure, deep tendon reflexes and (with high doses/renal impairment) for magnesium toxicity.

redFlags: Magnesium toxicity (loss of deep tendon reflexes, hypotension, respiratory depression, bradyarrhythmia) — stop the infusion; calcium gluconate is the antidote in severe toxicity.
Use caution and reduce dosing in renal impairment — magnesium accumulates.
Refractory hypokalaemia/hypocalcaemia often will not correct until magnesium is replaced.

references.label: SPS (NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service) — Treating acute hypomagnesaemia in adults

title: Puff adder (Bitis arietans) envenomation
summary: Heavy-bodied African viper responsible for a large share of severe envenomations in East Africa; predominantly cytotoxic with marked local swelling, blistering and tissue necrosis, and risk of hypovolaemic shock.

sections.heading: Species recognition
items: Bitis arietans — short, stout viper with distinctive chevron pattern; very widespread across Kenyan savanna, farmland and roadsides.
Slow-moving; relies on camouflage rather than flight, so step-on bites to the lower limb are typical.
Long, hinged fangs deliver large venom volumes — even adolescent puff adders can envenomate severely.

sections.heading: Clinical syndrome
items: Predominantly cytotoxic: rapid-onset local pain, progressive swelling extending up the limb over hours, bruising, blistering and tissue necrosis.
Systemic features: hypotension/hypovolaemic shock (capillary leak), nausea, vomiting; coagulopathy is uncommon but thrombocytopenia and DIC-like pictures are reported.
Onset of swelling within 30 minutes; peak local effects 24–48 h; necrosis evolves over days.
Acute kidney injury may follow shock or rhabdomyolysis.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: Mark the leading edge of swelling with a pen and time-stamp every 30–60 minutes.
Measure limb circumference at fixed points; reassess pulses, capillary refill and sensation hourly.
Check baseline FBC, U&E, creatinine, urinalysis (myoglobin), and a 20-minute whole blood clotting test (20WBCT).
Watch for compartment syndrome clinically (pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch) — confirm with compartment pressures before any fasciotomy.

sections.heading: Treatment
items: Antivenom: SAIMR polyvalent (covers Bitis arietans) for systemic envenomation or rapidly progressing local swelling crossing a joint.
Aggressive IV crystalloid resuscitation for hypotension; analgesia (paracetamol/opioid — avoid NSAIDs if any coagulopathy).
Elevate and immobilise the limb; do NOT apply tourniquets, incise, suck or apply ice.
Tetanus prophylaxis per status; antibiotics only for clinical infection, not prophylactically.

redFlags: Swelling crossing a major joint within 1 hour — give antivenom.
Hypotension, oliguria, altered consciousness — systemic envenomation.
Pain out of proportion, tense compartment, loss of distal pulses — assess for compartment syndrome before fasciotomy.
