MSF Snakebite Clinical Management — Sub-Saharan Africa
Warrell DA. Snake bite. Lancet 2010;375:77–88.
Spawls, Howell, Hinkel & Menegon. Field Guide to East African Reptiles.

title: Black mamba (Dendroaspis polylepis) envenomation
summary: Large, fast African elapid with potent neurotoxic venom; rapid-onset descending flaccid paralysis with airway and respiratory failure — antivenom plus early airway control are life-saving.

sections.heading: Species recognition
items: Dendroaspis polylepis — slate-grey terrestrial elapid up to 3 m; black inner mouth lining.
Found in savanna, rocky outcrops and lowland forest across East Africa; will defend itself vigorously if cornered.
Short, fixed fangs — bite may leave only faint marks but injects highly potent venom.

sections.heading: Clinical syndrome
items: Predominantly neurotoxic (alpha-neurotoxins + dendrotoxins): minimal local swelling, dry necrotic punctures.
Early: paraesthesia around mouth, metallic taste, sweating, hypersalivation, ptosis, blurred vision, dysphagia.
Progressive descending flaccid paralysis: bulbar weakness, then diaphragm — respiratory arrest possible within 30 minutes to a few hours.
Cardiovascular: tachycardia, hypertension, then bradyarrhythmias and shock in untreated cases.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: Continuous SpO2, cardiac monitor; nurse upright if airway adequate, supine with airway support if bulbar weakness.
Assess single-breath count, peak flow, ability to handle secretions and protect airway every 15 minutes early on.
Check pupil response, ptosis, neck flexion strength, gag reflex repeatedly — early bulbar signs predict respiratory failure.

sections.heading: Treatment
items: Airway first: intubate early at first sign of bulbar weakness or hypoventilation rather than waiting for arrest.
Antivenom: SAIMR polyvalent (covers all African mambas) — give without delay for any systemic neurotoxic feature.
Atropine + neostigmine trial may transiently improve symptoms (post-synaptic neurotoxin component) but is NOT a substitute for antivenom and intubation.
Pressure-immobilisation bandage is reasonable pre-hospital for neurotoxic elapid bites — do not delay transport.

redFlags: Ptosis, dysarthria, dysphagia or single-breath count under 20 — intubate now.
Apnoea pre-hospital — bag-valve-mask ventilation continued until antivenom and intubation in hospital.
Cardiac arrest in a young patient post-mamba bite — prolonged resuscitation can succeed because neurotoxins are reversible.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Prevention and Clinical Management of Snakebite in Africa (2010)
MSF Snakebite Clinical Management — Sub-Saharan Africa
Theakston RDG, Warrell DA. Antivenoms for the treatment of snake bite envenoming.

title: Green mamba (Dendroaspis angusticeps) envenomation
summary: Arboreal East African elapid with neurotoxic venom; presentations are usually less explosive than black mamba but still risk airway and respiratory compromise.

sections.heading: Species recognition
items: Dendroaspis angusticeps — bright green, slender arboreal snake of coastal forest and woodland in Kenya/Tanzania.
Largely tree-dwelling; bites tend to involve upper limb or head/neck when handling vegetation.
Often confused with non-venomous green snakes — assume venomous if not confidently identified.

sections.heading: Clinical syndrome
items: Neurotoxic but generally less rapid than black mamba: ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, dysphagia and limb weakness over hours.
Local effects: mild pain and swelling; necrosis uncommon.
Cardiovascular features (tachycardia, hypertension) reported but usually milder.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: Serial neuromuscular junction assessment: ptosis, extra-ocular movements, neck flexion, single-breath count.
Continuous SpO2 and cardiac monitor; minimum 24 hours observation even if asymptomatic at presentation.

sections.heading: Treatment
items: Antivenom: SAIMR polyvalent (covers green mamba) for any systemic neurotoxic sign.
Early airway protection if bulbar weakness; mechanical ventilation if respiratory failure.
Pressure-immobilisation bandage may be considered pre-hospital.

redFlags: Progressive ptosis or dysphagia — antivenom and prepare for intubation.
Even apparently mild envenomation can deteriorate over hours — do not discharge before 24 h observation.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Prevention and Clinical Management of Snakebite in Africa (2010)
MSF Snakebite Clinical Management — Sub-Saharan Africa
Spawls et al. Field Guide to East African Reptiles.

title: Forest cobra (Naja melanoleuca) envenomation
summary: Large African cobra of forest and forest-edge habitats with predominantly neurotoxic venom; potential for severe descending paralysis and respiratory failure.

sections.heading: Species recognition
items: Naja melanoleuca — large glossy black cobra (lighter throat with dark bands) of forest, swamp and coastal bush in East Africa.
Strong swimmer; can be encountered in/near water.
Hooded display when threatened; does NOT spit.

sections.heading: Clinical syndrome
items: Predominantly neurotoxic with some local effects: pain and modest swelling at bite site, ptosis, dysphagia, descending paralysis.
Onset typically within 1–4 hours; respiratory failure if untreated.
Local necrosis less prominent than in spitting cobras but can occur.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: Repeated NMJ assessment as for other neurotoxic elapids; SpO2 and cardiac monitoring.
Mark and monitor any local swelling.

sections.heading: Treatment
items: Antivenom: SAIMR polyvalent (covers Naja melanoleuca).
Intubate early for bulbar weakness; supportive ventilation until paralysis resolves.
Local wound care; tetanus prophylaxis.

redFlags: Ptosis, dysphagia or hypoventilation — antivenom and airway control without delay.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Prevention and Clinical Management of Snakebite in Africa (2010)
MSF Snakebite Clinical Management — Sub-Saharan Africa

title: Red spitting cobra (Naja pallida) envenomation
summary: East African spitting cobra causing cytotoxic local injury from bites and severe ocular injury from venom-spray into the eyes; eye decontamination is the immediate priority for spray injuries.

sections.heading: Species recognition
items: Naja pallida — slim cobra, colour red-orange to pink-grey with dark throat band, widespread in dry lowlands of northern and eastern Kenya.
Can spit venom 2–3 m towards eyes when threatened.
Bites typically on lower limb; spray injuries usually to face/eyes.

sections.heading: Clinical syndrome
items: Bite: predominantly cytotoxic — pain, swelling, blistering and risk of necrosis; systemic neurotoxicity is rare but possible.
Eye exposure: intense pain, blepharospasm, chemosis, corneal abrasion/ulceration, risk of permanent visual impairment if not irrigated.
Anaphylactoid features (urticaria, bronchospasm) reported in some cases.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: For bites: monitor local progression as for any cytotoxic envenomation (mark swelling, measure circumference, observe for necrosis).
For eye exposure: visual acuity, fluorescein staining, slit-lamp examination after irrigation; ophthalmology review if corneal defect.

sections.heading: Treatment
items: Eye exposure — irrigate immediately with copious clean water, 0.9% saline or any potable fluid for at least 15–20 minutes before any other intervention.
After irrigation: topical antibiotic (e.g. chloramphenicol drops) and analgesia; mydriatic (cyclopentolate) for ciliary spasm; tetanus per status.
For bites with progressive swelling or systemic signs: SAIMR polyvalent antivenom.
Do NOT instil antivenom into the eye — not indicated, may worsen inflammation.

redFlags: Corneal defect, hypopyon, persistent visual loss — urgent ophthalmology.
Rapidly extending swelling, blistering or necrosis after bite — give antivenom.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Prevention and Clinical Management of Snakebite in Africa (2010)
MSF Snakebite Clinical Management — Sub-Saharan Africa
Warrell DA. Venomous bites, stings and poisoning. Infect Dis Clin North Am 2012.

title: Black-necked spitting cobra (Naja nigricollis) envenomation
summary: Widespread African spitting cobra responsible for many cytotoxic bites and ocular venom-spray injuries in East Africa; bites cause severe local tissue damage and may require antivenom even without systemic neurotoxicity.

sections.heading: Species recognition
items: Naja nigricollis — variable in colour (olive, grey, brown to black) with a dark band on the throat; common in savanna and farmland.
Frequently spits venom in defensive display; bites typically on lower limb in adults, head/upper body in children.

sections.heading: Clinical syndrome
items: Bite: prominent cytotoxicity — early pain, rapidly progressing swelling, blistering and tissue necrosis; systemic neurotoxicity rare.
Necrosis can be extensive and lead to limb-threatening tissue loss if untreated.
Eye exposure: severe chemical conjunctivitis, corneal injury as with N. pallida.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: Mark and time-stamp leading edge of swelling; measure limb circumference serially.
Daily wound review for necrosis evolution; baseline FBC, U&E, creatinine.
If eye exposed: visual acuity, fluorescein, slit-lamp after irrigation.

sections.heading: Treatment
items: Antivenom: SAIMR polyvalent for any progressive swelling crossing a joint, systemic features or bites in children.
Eye exposure: copious irrigation for 15–20 minutes, then topical antibiotic, analgesia and ophthalmology review.
Conservative wound management initially; delayed surgical debridement for clearly demarcated necrosis after antivenom and resuscitation.
Do NOT perform prophylactic fasciotomy — most apparent compartment syndromes in cobra bites are due to subcutaneous oedema, not raised compartment pressure.

redFlags: Progressive necrosis after 48 hours — surgical review.
Concomitant systemic infection (sepsis from devitalised tissue) — broad-spectrum antibiotics and source control.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Prevention and Clinical Management of Snakebite in Africa (2010)
MSF Snakebite Clinical Management — Sub-Saharan Africa

title: Egyptian cobra (Naja haje) envenomation
summary: Large North-East African cobra (present in northern Kenya) with predominantly neurotoxic venom; severe descending paralysis and respiratory failure possible.

sections.heading: Species recognition
items: Naja haje — large, heavy cobra, brown to dark-brown; occurs in arid and semi-arid northern Kenya and adjacent Horn of Africa.
Does NOT spit; relies on hooded display and bite.

sections.heading: Clinical syndrome
items: Predominantly neurotoxic: ptosis, dysphagia, ophthalmoplegia, descending paralysis with respiratory failure.
Local effects: pain, modest swelling, occasional necrosis.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: NMJ assessment, SpO2, cardiac monitor; minimum 24 h observation.

sections.heading: Treatment
items: Antivenom: SAIMR polyvalent (covers Naja haje).
Early intubation for bulbar weakness; supportive ventilation.
Wound care, tetanus prophylaxis.

redFlags: Bulbar weakness or hypoventilation — antivenom and airway control.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Prevention and Clinical Management of Snakebite in Africa (2010)
MSF Snakebite Clinical Management — Sub-Saharan Africa

title: Saw-scaled viper (Echis pyramidum) envenomation
summary: Small but highly venomous viper of dry northern Kenya causing severe consumption coagulopathy; antivenom is indicated for any incoagulable blood on the 20-minute whole blood clotting test.

sections.heading: Species recognition
items: Echis pyramidum (and related Echis spp.) — small, pale viper with rough keeled scales that rub together producing a rasping warning sound.
Found in arid and semi-arid northern and north-eastern Kenya; nocturnal and well-camouflaged.

sections.heading: Clinical syndrome
items: Predominantly haemotoxic: venom-induced consumption coagulopathy (low fibrinogen), thrombocytopenia and spontaneous bleeding — gums, nose, wound, urine, gut, intracranial.
Local effects: pain, modest swelling; necrosis less prominent than in puff adder bites.
Onset of coagulopathy within hours, persisting days; AKI from haemoglobinuria/shock.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: 20-minute whole blood clotting test (20WBCT) at presentation and every 6 hours until normal for 24 h.
Daily FBC, fibrinogen if available, U&E, creatinine, urinalysis.
Watch for bleeding from gums, GI tract, urine, intracranial signs (headache, focal deficit, reduced GCS).

sections.heading: Treatment
items: Antivenom: SAIMR polyvalent (covers Echis ocellatus type but limited efficacy against some Echis spp.) OR specific viperid antivenom that covers Echis pyramidum (e.g. EchiTAb-Plus-ICP / FAV-Afrique where available) — choose product per local availability and label.
Repeat antivenom dose if 20WBCT remains unclotted 6 hours after the first dose.
Avoid IM injections, NSAIDs, aspirin and heparin during coagulopathy.
Blood products (FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets) only after adequate antivenom — clotting factors are otherwise consumed.

redFlags: Unclotted 20WBCT — give antivenom regardless of swelling.
Headache, vomiting, focal neurology — exclude intracranial haemorrhage.
Active bleeding despite antivenom — repeat dose, then blood products.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Prevention and Clinical Management of Snakebite in Africa (2010)
MSF Snakebite Clinical Management — Sub-Saharan Africa
Warrell DA. Snake bite. Lancet 2010;375:77–88.

title: Boomslang (Dispholidus typus) envenomation
summary: Rear-fanged arboreal colubrid whose venom causes a profound, often delayed consumption coagulopathy — antivenom is required even in apparently mild cases because catastrophic bleeding can present days later.

sections.heading: Species recognition
items: Dispholidus typus — slender arboreal snake, large eyes, colour varies (bright green males, brown females/juveniles), present across East African woodland and coastal forest.
Rear-fanged with large gape; bites are uncommon but underestimated.
Often misidentified as a harmless tree snake — assume potentially lethal.

sections.heading: Clinical syndrome
items: Predominantly haemotoxic: delayed onset (often 24–72 hours, occasionally up to 5 days) of severe consumption coagulopathy.
Bleeding: gum oozing, epistaxis, haematuria, GI bleeding, intracranial haemorrhage; haemolysis and AKI may follow.
Local effects minimal — small bite marks, little swelling — falsely reassuring.
Twig snake (Thelotornis) envenomation produces an identical syndrome and is managed similarly.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: 20WBCT at presentation and every 6 hours for at least 48–72 hours given delayed onset; daily FBC, U&E, creatinine.
Admit any confirmed boomslang bite for a minimum of 48 hours even if asymptomatic and 20WBCT initially normal.

sections.heading: Treatment
items: Antivenom: SAIMR monovalent boomslang antivenom is the ONLY effective product — SAIMR polyvalent does NOT cover Dispholidus.
Give boomslang antivenom for any confirmed bite with coagulopathy; supply may be limited and central blood-bank stocked.
Supportive care: blood products (FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets, packed cells) after antivenom.
Avoid IM injections and NSAIDs/aspirin/heparin.

redFlags: Any bleeding at all in a confirmed boomslang bite — life-threatening coagulopathy.
Polyvalent antivenom alone — INADEQUATE for boomslang; obtain monovalent product.
Discharge before 48–72 hours observation — coagulopathy can present late.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Prevention and Clinical Management of Snakebite in Africa (2010)
MSF Snakebite Clinical Management — Sub-Saharan Africa
SAVP (South African Vaccine Producers) Boomslang antivenom product information.

title: Twig snake / vine snake (Thelotornis spp.) envenomation
summary: Slender arboreal rear-fanged colubrid whose venom produces a delayed boomslang-like consumption coagulopathy; there is no commercially available specific antivenom and management is largely supportive.

sections.heading: Species recognition
items: Thelotornis spp. — extremely slender, twig-mimicking arboreal snake with elongated head and keyhole pupil.
Present in woodland and coastal forest; often handled because mistaken for a harmless vine snake.

sections.heading: Clinical syndrome
items: Predominantly haemotoxic with delayed onset (24–72 h or longer) consumption coagulopathy — clinically identical to boomslang.
Bleeding: mucosal, GI, haematuria, intracranial; haemolysis and AKI may follow.
Local signs minimal.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: 20WBCT every 6 hours for at least 48–72 hours; daily FBC, U&E, creatinine.
Admit for minimum 48–72 hours observation.

sections.heading: Treatment
items: No effective commercial antivenom — SAIMR polyvalent and boomslang monovalent are NOT proven effective for Thelotornis.
Supportive: FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets, packed cells for active bleeding or severe coagulopathy.
Avoid NSAIDs, aspirin, heparin and IM injections.

redFlags: Any spontaneous bleeding — escalate to blood products and intensive monitoring.
Falsely reassuring early presentation — coagulopathy can be late and catastrophic.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Prevention and Clinical Management of Snakebite in Africa (2010)
MSF Snakebite Clinical Management — Sub-Saharan Africa

title: Rinkhals (Hemachatus haemachatus) envenomation
summary: Southern African spitting elapid (range edges into East Africa) producing a mixed cytotoxic and neurotoxic envenomation, plus risk of ocular injury from venom spray.

sections.heading: Species recognition
items: Hemachatus haemachatus — keeled-scaled cobra-like elapid, dark above with throat bands; may feign death.
Can spit venom several metres towards eyes.

sections.heading: Clinical syndrome
items: Mixed cytotoxic and neurotoxic: local swelling and pain plus possible ptosis, dysphagia and respiratory weakness.
Eye exposure: severe conjunctivitis, corneal injury similar to Naja spitting cobras.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: Mark swelling; NMJ assessment and SpO2/cardiac monitor.
Ocular exam after irrigation if spray exposure.

sections.heading: Treatment
items: Antivenom: SAIMR polyvalent (covers Hemachatus) for progressive swelling or any neurotoxic feature.
Eye spray: copious irrigation, topical antibiotic, ophthalmology review.
Airway support as needed.

redFlags: Bulbar weakness or hypoventilation — early intubation.
Corneal defect after spray — ophthalmology review.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Prevention and Clinical Management of Snakebite in Africa (2010)
MSF Snakebite Clinical Management — Sub-Saharan Africa

title: Night adder (Causus rhombeatus and related spp.) envenomation
summary: Small African viper whose bites produce painful but generally milder cytotoxic envenomation; severe systemic effects and necrosis are uncommon and most cases need only supportive care.

sections.heading: Species recognition
items: Causus rhombeatus and related Causus spp. — small, stout, often rhomboid-patterned viper of damp grassland and farmland across East Africa.
Active by day and night; bites common around homesteads.

sections.heading: Clinical syndrome
items: Local: pain, swelling, lymphadenopathy and bruising — typically self-limiting over 2–5 days.
Systemic features uncommon; significant necrosis or coagulopathy rare.
Children and frail patients can still develop clinically significant swelling.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: Mark and time-stamp swelling; observe at minimum 12–24 hours.
Baseline 20WBCT and FBC; routine repeat not required if normal and patient asymptomatic.

sections.heading: Treatment
items: Most cases: supportive care only — analgesia, limb elevation, tetanus prophylaxis.
Antivenom rarely indicated and is NOT used routinely for Causus envenomation; reserve for unusual systemic features or severe progressive swelling and discuss with toxicology/poison centre.

redFlags: Unusually rapid systemic progression — reassess species identification.
Bites in children, pregnancy or significant comorbidity — lower threshold for admission.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Prevention and Clinical Management of Snakebite in Africa (2010)
MSF Snakebite Clinical Management — Sub-Saharan Africa
Spawls et al. Field Guide to East African Reptiles.

title: Snake envenomation syndrome recognition
summary: Pattern-based classification of African snakebite into cytotoxic, neurotoxic and haemotoxic (and mixed) syndromes — used to guide antivenom indication and monitoring when the snake itself was not identified.

sections.heading: Cytotoxic syndrome
items: Features: marked local pain, progressive swelling, blistering, ecchymosis, lymphadenopathy, possible necrosis.
Systemic: hypovolaemia from capillary leak; coagulopathy usually absent or mild.
Likely species in East Africa: puff adder (Bitis arietans), spitting cobras (Naja nigricollis, N. pallida), gaboon viper.

sections.heading: Neurotoxic syndrome
items: Features: ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, dysarthria, dysphagia, descending flaccid paralysis, respiratory failure.
Local effects often minimal — dry punctures may belie severe systemic envenomation.
Likely species: mambas (Dendroaspis spp.), non-spitting cobras (Naja melanoleuca, N. haje).

sections.heading: Haemotoxic syndrome
items: Features: spontaneous bleeding (gums, epistaxis, haematuria, GI, intracranial) and incoagulable blood on 20WBCT.
Onset can be rapid (Echis) or DELAYED 24–72 h or more (boomslang, twig snake).
Likely species: saw-scaled vipers (Echis spp.), boomslang (Dispholidus typus), twig snake (Thelotornis spp.).

sections.heading: Mixed syndromes
items: Cyto + neuro: rinkhals (Hemachatus), occasional spitting cobra cases.
Cyto + mild coagulopathy: severe puff adder envenomation can show secondary DIC-like changes.
When syndrome unclear, treat by pattern recognition — antivenom is indicated by syndrome, not species ID.

sections.heading: Operational rule
items: Identification of the species is helpful but NOT required to treat — syndrome-based management is the WHO recommendation.
Do not delay antivenom waiting for species ID, photographs or the dead snake.

redFlags: Any neurotoxic sign — high lethality without airway support and antivenom.
Incoagulable blood — give antivenom even without overt bleeding.
Swelling crossing a major joint within an hour — systemic envenomation likely.

title: 20-minute whole blood clotting test (20WBCT)
summary: WHO bedside test to detect venom-induced consumption coagulopathy in snakebite using a clean, dry glass tube — incoagulable blood at 20 minutes is an indication for antivenom regardless of species.

sections.heading: Equipment
items: A NEW, clean and DRY glass test tube (not plastic — clotting depends on contact activation by glass).
Syringe and needle for venepuncture; no anticoagulant.
Timer (20 minutes).

sections.heading: Procedure
items: Draw a few millilitres (about 2 mL) of fresh venous blood by clean venepuncture.
Place the blood directly into the clean, dry glass tube — do NOT add any anticoagulant.
Leave the tube undisturbed and upright at room temperature for exactly 20 minutes — do NOT shake or tip during this time.
After 20 minutes, tilt the tube once and observe the contents.

sections.heading: Interpretation
items: Solid clot that does not run when the tube is tipped — NORMAL clotting.
Liquid blood (no clot, or only a wisp of fibrin) — INCOAGULABLE BLOOD: indicates venom-induced consumption coagulopathy.
Incoagulable blood is an indication for antivenom regardless of species or local features.
Repeat 20WBCT every 6 hours after antivenom until normal for 24 hours; repeat at 24 h and 48 h in suspected boomslang/twig snake bites even if initially normal.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
items: Plastic or pre-treated tubes — falsely prolonged clotting (uninterpretable).
Disturbing the tube before 20 minutes — falsely prolonged result.
A poorly performed venepuncture (slow draw, multiple attempts) can underestimate coagulopathy — repeat if uncertain.
The 20WBCT detects gross afibrinogenaemia; it does NOT reliably detect milder coagulopathy — a normal 20WBCT does not exclude all venom effects.

redFlags: Incoagulable blood — give antivenom; avoid IM injections and arterial sampling.
Persistently incoagulable blood 6 hours after antivenom — repeat antivenom dose.

title: Indications for antivenom in African snakebite
summary: Antivenom is reserved for systemic envenomation or severe progressive local envenomation — the majority of snakebites are dry or minor and do NOT need antivenom, which carries real anaphylaxis risk.

sections.heading: When antivenom IS indicated (any one)
items: Any sign of systemic envenomation: neurotoxic (ptosis, dysphagia, respiratory weakness), haemotoxic (spontaneous bleeding or incoagulable 20WBCT), shock, AKI, haemoglobinuria, rhabdomyolysis.
Severe/progressive local envenomation: swelling crossing a major joint within 1–2 hours, swelling involving more than half the bitten limb, marked rapid bruising.
Bite by a snake known to produce delayed coagulopathy (boomslang, twig snake) — even if currently asymptomatic, once any coagulopathy appears.
Bite to a high-risk site (face, neck, hand) in a child with rapid local progression.

sections.heading: When antivenom is NOT indicated
items: Asymptomatic 'dry bite' with no local swelling, normal vital signs and normal 20WBCT after appropriate observation.
Minimal local swelling that is not progressive and is confined to the bite site after several hours.
Bite by a non-venomous snake (confirmed by reliable identification).
Causus / night adder bites typically — supportive care only.

sections.heading: Decision principles
items: Up to 50% of viperid bites and a higher proportion of elapid 'bites' may be dry — withholding antivenom in genuinely asymptomatic patients is appropriate and reduces preventable anaphylaxis.
Observe asymptomatic patients for at least 24 hours with serial examination and 20WBCT before discharge.
Indication is based on syndrome and progression, not on the patient's anxiety or the visual appearance of the bite alone.

redFlags: Delayed coagulopathy can appear at 24–72 hours after boomslang/twig snake bites — do not stop monitoring early.
Children and pregnant women can deteriorate faster — lower threshold for antivenom.

title: Antivenom administration (SAIMR polyvalent)
summary: Practical administration of polyvalent equine antivenom for systemic African snakebite envenomation — IV infusion under close monitoring, with adrenaline drawn up and ready for the inevitable risk of anaphylaxis.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Confirm an indication for antivenom (see 'envenomation-antivenom-indications').
Use SAIMR polyvalent antivenom for most African bites EXCEPT boomslang (use monovalent boomslang antivenom).
Initial dose for adults with systemic envenomation is typically 80–100 mL (8–10 vials) of SAIMR polyvalent — confirm against current product label.
Paediatric dose is the SAME as adult — antivenom neutralises a venom dose, not body weight.
Reconstitute lyophilised product per label; dilute in 200–500 mL 0.9% saline for IV infusion.

sections.heading: Pre-administration
items: Secure two IV lines; ensure resuscitation drugs and adrenaline IM 1:1000 (0.5 mg adult, 0.01 mg/kg child) are drawn up at the bedside.
Continuous monitoring: SpO2, BP, HR, RR; staff available to manage anaphylaxis.

Routine prophylactic adrenaline subcutaneously before antivenom is controversial and not universally recommended — follow current local guideline; do NOT give corticosteroids or antihistamines as routine premedication unless local protocol explicitly directs it.

sections.heading: Infusion
items: Start the infusion slowly over the first 10–15 minutes while observing closely for an early reaction.
If no reaction, complete the full dose over 30–60 minutes.
Repeat the dose after 6 hours if 20WBCT remains incoagulable or systemic features persist/recur (neurotoxic or haemotoxic).
Do NOT inject antivenom locally into the bite site — ineffective and harmful.

sections.heading: After administration
items: Continue monitoring for 24 hours minimum; serial 20WBCT for haemotoxic syndromes; NMJ checks for neurotoxic.
Warn the patient about serum sickness presenting 5–14 days later (urticaria, fever, arthralgia) and how to seek care.

redFlags: Anaphylaxis during infusion — pause, give IM adrenaline, manage airway, then resume slowly when stable.
Persistent envenomation 6 hours after the first dose — repeat antivenom.

title: Anaphylaxis during antivenom infusion
summary: Early acute reactions to equine antivenom are common; the standard response is to pause the infusion, treat anaphylaxis with IM adrenaline, then restart the antivenom slowly because the patient still needs the venom neutralised.

sections.heading: Recognition
items: Early features: urticaria, flushing, pruritus, cough, bronchospasm, hypotension, tachycardia, vomiting, angio-oedema.
Most reactions occur within the first 30–60 minutes of infusion.
Reactions are pharmacologically distinct from venom effects and require specific treatment.

sections.heading: Immediate actions
items: PAUSE the antivenom infusion (do not discontinue permanently — the patient still needs it).
Give IM adrenaline 1:1000: adult 0.5 mg (0.5 mL); child 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) into the anterolateral thigh; repeat every 5 minutes as needed.
Position supine with legs raised (if tolerated and no airway compromise); high-flow oxygen.
IV crystalloid bolus 20 mL/kg for hypotension.
Bronchospasm: nebulised salbutamol.
Antihistamine (e.g. chlorphenamine IV) and hydrocortisone IV are adjuncts AFTER adrenaline — never substitute for it.

sections.heading: Restarting the antivenom
items: Once the patient is haemodynamically stable and symptoms have settled, RESTART the antivenom at a much slower rate.
Continue to monitor closely; further small doses of adrenaline and antihistamine may be needed.
Do NOT abandon antivenom in a patient with genuine systemic envenomation — the alternative (untreated envenomation) is more dangerous than the reaction.

redFlags: Stridor, severe bronchospasm or shock — IM adrenaline immediately; consider IV adrenaline infusion in monitored setting only.
Biphasic reaction up to several hours later — keep adrenaline drawn up at the bedside.

title: Serum sickness after antivenom
summary: Type III hypersensitivity reaction occurring 5–14 days after equine antivenom — urticaria, fever, arthralgia and lymphadenopathy — usually self-limiting and responsive to oral antihistamines and a short course of prednisolone.

sections.heading: Clinical features
items: Onset 5–14 days after antivenom administration.
Urticaria, fever, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy, sometimes proteinuria, less commonly nephritis.
Self-limiting in most cases but can be prolonged.

sections.heading: Management
items: Oral antihistamine for symptomatic urticaria/pruritus.
Oral prednisolone for moderate/severe symptoms — typical course is a short tapering course (e.g. prednisolone 5 days then taper) per local guideline.
Analgesia for arthralgia.
Most patients can be managed as outpatients with safety-netting.

sections.heading: Counselling at discharge after antivenom
items: Warn every patient receiving antivenom about possible serum sickness and to return if rash, fever, joint pain or face swelling appear in the next 2 weeks.
Document the antivenom product, batch and date in the patient's record.

redFlags: Renal involvement (significant proteinuria, AKI) — escalate.
Severe systemic features (e.g. vasculitis) — referral to specialist.

title: Airway and ventilation in neurotoxic envenomation
summary: Mamba and non-spitting cobra envenomation cause descending paralysis and respiratory arrest; early elective intubation before bulbar collapse and supportive ventilation until neurotoxin clears is the key to survival.

sections.heading: Recognition of impending respiratory failure
items: Early: ptosis, blurred vision, dysarthria, hypersalivation, jaw weakness, dysphagia.
Late: poor cough, single-breath count under 20, shallow tachypnoea, paradoxical abdominal movement, SpO2 fall.
Patient can appear deceptively calm until sudden decompensation.

sections.heading: Management
items: Position upright if able to protect airway; supine with airway support if bulbar weakness.
Intubate ELECTIVELY at first sign of bulbar weakness or significant respiratory muscle weakness — do not wait for arrest.
Use standard rapid sequence intubation drugs; avoid prolonged-acting non-depolarising NMBAs where possible (effects superimpose on neurotoxin).
Mechanical ventilation until paralysis resolves — this can take hours to days.
Antivenom (SAIMR polyvalent) is the definitive treatment; supportive ventilation buys time for it to work.

Atropine + neostigmine trial: in cobra (post-synaptic) neurotoxicity, a trial may produce transient improvement — administer per local protocol, but do not delay antivenom or intubation while observing the response.

sections.heading: Ongoing care
items: Nasogastric tube for nutrition; eye care; pressure-area care; VTE prophylaxis.
Daily assessment for return of muscle strength: spontaneous eye opening, hand grip, head lift, single-breath count.
Wean and extubate once respiratory muscle strength has clearly returned (sustained head lift, single-breath count above 25).

redFlags: Sudden apnoea — bag-valve-mask ventilation, intubate immediately.
Cardiac arrest after mamba bite — prolonged resuscitation can succeed; neurotoxicity is reversible.

title: Cytotoxic snakebite wound management
summary: Most apparent compartment syndromes after cytotoxic snakebites are subcutaneous oedema, not true raised compartment pressure — antivenom and conservative wound care first; surgical debridement only when demarcated necrosis is established.

sections.heading: Initial wound assessment
items: Clean the bite site gently with water/saline; do not incise, suck or apply ice.
Mark the leading edge of swelling and measure limb circumference at fixed points.
Photograph and document blistering, ecchymosis, demarcation lines.

sections.heading: Conservative management
items: Elevate and immobilise the limb in a splint at functional position.
Analgesia (paracetamol/opioid); avoid NSAIDs if any coagulopathy.
Tetanus prophylaxis per status.

Antibiotics are NOT routinely indicated — give only for clinical evidence of secondary infection (cellulitis, abscess, systemic sepsis), and choose cover for skin pathogens and anaerobes per local sensitivities.

sections.heading: Compartment syndrome
items: True compartment syndrome is UNCOMMON in African snakebite — most tense, swollen limbs are subcutaneous oedema.

Diagnose clinically (pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense compartments, distal neuro deficit) AND with measured compartment pressure where available (>30–40 mmHg or within 30 mmHg of diastolic BP).
Give antivenom FIRST and correct coagulopathy before any consideration of fasciotomy.
Prophylactic fasciotomy is contraindicated — it can cause severe bleeding in coagulopathic patients without improving outcome.

sections.heading: Surgical debridement
items: Delay surgical debridement until necrosis is clearly demarcated (typically several days).
Excise frankly necrotic tissue; leave viable tissue.
Plan reconstruction (skin grafting, flap) once wound bed is clean and granulating.

redFlags: Pain out of proportion AND measured compartment pressure raised — compartment syndrome warrants fasciotomy after antivenom and correction of coagulopathy.
Spreading cellulitis, abscess or systemic sepsis — antibiotics and source control.

title: Coagulopathy monitoring and blood products in snakebite
summary: Venom-induced consumption coagulopathy is monitored at the bedside with the 20WBCT; antivenom is the definitive treatment, and blood products are reserved for active bleeding or persistent coagulopathy AFTER adequate antivenom.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: Perform 20WBCT at presentation and every 6 hours until normal for 24 hours.
Daily FBC, U&E, creatinine; fibrinogen and PT/INR if available.
For suspected boomslang or twig snake bite, repeat 20WBCT every 6 h for at least 48–72 hours even if initially normal.

sections.heading: Antivenom
items: Incoagulable 20WBCT is itself an indication for antivenom regardless of local features.
Repeat antivenom dose after 6 hours if 20WBCT remains incoagulable.
Coagulation typically restores within 6 hours of adequate antivenom — persistent incoagulability suggests inadequate dose or wrong antivenom.

sections.heading: Blood products
items: Give blood products only AFTER antivenom — otherwise clotting factors are consumed by circulating venom.
Fresh frozen plasma 10–15 mL/kg for ongoing bleeding with abnormal coagulation.
Cryoprecipitate for low fibrinogen.
Platelets for clinically significant thrombocytopenia with bleeding.
Packed red cells for symptomatic anaemia or large-volume loss.

sections.heading: Avoid
items: IM injections (haematoma), arterial puncture and central venous lines in non-compressible sites while coagulopathic.
Aspirin, NSAIDs, heparin and other antiplatelet/anticoagulant drugs.
Routine tranexamic acid is not recommended specifically for snake venom coagulopathy outside trial settings — follow local guidance.

redFlags: Intracranial bleeding signs (headache, vomiting, focal deficit, reduced GCS) — urgent imaging and resuscitation.
Persistent incoagulable blood 6 hours after antivenom — repeat antivenom and reassess product choice.

title: Eye decontamination after spitting cobra venom exposure
summary: Spitting cobra venom in the eye is an ocular chemical emergency — immediate copious irrigation with water or saline takes priority over every other intervention, including history-taking.

sections.heading: Immediate first aid (pre-hospital and at triage)
items: Irrigate the affected eye(s) IMMEDIATELY with the cleanest fluid available — clean water, 0.9% saline, bottled water or even milk.
Hold the eyelids open and run fluid across the eye from the inner to the outer canthus for at least 15–20 minutes.
Do NOT delay irrigation to find sterile fluid — any clean potable fluid is better than none.

sections.heading: In-hospital assessment after irrigation
items: Test visual acuity in each eye.
Topical anaesthetic to allow examination if blepharospasm is severe.
Fluorescein staining and slit-lamp examination for corneal abrasions or ulceration.
Document any persistent visual deficit.

sections.heading: Ongoing care
items: Topical antibiotic (e.g. chloramphenicol drops or ointment) for corneal injury.
Cycloplegic (e.g. cyclopentolate) for ciliary spasm and photophobia if significant.
Oral analgesia.
Tetanus prophylaxis per status.
Ophthalmology review for any corneal defect, persistent pain or visual loss.

sections.heading: What NOT to do
items: Do NOT instil systemic antivenom into the eye — not indicated and may worsen inflammation.
Do NOT use topical steroids without ophthalmology advice — risk of worsening epithelial defect or infection.
Do NOT delay irrigation while obtaining 'better' fluid — time to irrigation determines outcome.

redFlags: Persistent visual loss, hypopyon, deep corneal ulceration — urgent ophthalmology.
Bilateral eye exposure — irrigate both eyes simultaneously.

title: Pre-hospital first aid for snakebite
summary: Practical pre-hospital first aid for African snakebite: reassure and immobilise the victim, remove constricting items, and transport rapidly to a health facility — and avoid the traditional measures (cuts, tourniquets, suction) that cause more harm than the bite.

sections.heading: Do
items: Move the victim away from the snake; ensure rescuer safety.
Reassure — fear and excitement increase venom spread; explain the journey.
Immobilise the bitten limb in a functional position with a splint and keep the patient as still as possible.
Remove rings, watches, bangles and tight clothing from the bitten limb BEFORE swelling worsens.
Transport to the nearest facility with antivenom capability as quickly as is safe.
If the snake is dead and can be brought safely, do so for identification — but do NOT delay transport, and do NOT handle a 'dead' snake with bare hands (reflex bites occur).

sections.heading: Do NOT
items: Do NOT make incisions over the bite site.
Do NOT attempt suction (mouth, syringe or commercial 'extractor' devices).
Do NOT apply arterial tourniquets — they cause ischaemia and concentrate venom, increasing necrosis.
Do NOT apply ice, heat, electric shock or chemicals to the wound.
Do NOT give alcohol, sedatives or aspirin/NSAIDs.
Do NOT cauterise or apply traditional remedies (herbal poultices, snake stones) — these delay definitive care and can introduce infection.

sections.heading: Pressure-immobilisation bandage (selected cases)
items: A correctly applied pressure-immobilisation bandage (broad firm crepe bandage from distal to proximal, plus splint) is acceptable for NEUROTOXIC ELAPID bites (mamba, non-spitting cobra) where transport time is significant.
Should NOT be used routinely for cytotoxic viperid bites in Africa because it may concentrate cytotoxic venom and worsen local injury.
If applied, do NOT remove it until antivenom is available and the patient is being actively monitored.

redFlags: Tourniquet already applied in the field — release SLOWLY in a monitored environment, with antivenom and resuscitation ready (sudden release can precipitate shock).
Bite to face/neck — anticipate airway compromise on transport.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Prevention and Clinical Management of Snakebite in Africa (2010)

title: Pressure-immobilisation bandage technique
summary: Pressure-immobilisation bandaging delays systemic spread of neurotoxic venoms by limiting lymphatic flow; indicated mainly for neurotoxic elapid (mamba, non-spitting cobra) bites in Africa, NOT routinely for cytotoxic viperid bites.

sections.heading: Indications
items: Confirmed or strongly suspected bite by a neurotoxic elapid (mamba, non-spitting cobra) where transport to definitive care will take significant time.
Not routinely recommended for cytotoxic viperid (puff adder, spitting cobra) bites — may worsen local injury.

sections.heading: Technique
items: Use a broad (10–15 cm) firm crepe or elasticated bandage.
Start at the bite site and bandage firmly distal-to-proximal up the entire limb, with the same pressure as for a sprained ankle (firm but distal pulses preserved).
Apply a splint (e.g. wooden board, rolled magazine) along the limb to keep it rigid; bandage the splint in place.
Keep the limb at or below heart level; keep the patient still — carry rather than walk if possible.
Mark the bite site location on the bandage with a pen so it can be found later without removal.

sections.heading: After arrival
items: Do NOT remove the bandage until antivenom is available, IV access is in place and the patient is on monitoring — sudden removal can precipitate rapid systemic envenomation.
If bandage was applied for a cytotoxic bite by mistake, monitor the limb and reassess the indication; remove with same precautions as above.

redFlags: Loss of distal pulses, severe pain or progressive cyanosis distal to the bandage — bandage is too tight; loosen slightly under monitoring.
Patient deteriorates suddenly on bandage release — be ready with antivenom and resuscitation.

title: Paediatric snakebite considerations
summary: Children receive the SAME antivenom dose as adults because antivenom is dosed against venom mass — they get the same envenoming dose from a single bite but distribute it through a smaller body, so they often deteriorate faster.

sections.heading: Key principles
items: Children receive the SAME initial antivenom dose as adults (e.g. SAIMR polyvalent 80–100 mL initial dose) — do NOT reduce by weight.
Higher relative venom load per kg means children may deteriorate faster and more dramatically than adults.
Bites to small extremities (hand, foot, face) carry higher risk of severe local injury and airway compromise.

sections.heading: Resuscitation
items: IV access can be difficult in shock — intraosseous access is acceptable.
Crystalloid bolus 10–20 mL/kg titrated to perfusion.
Adrenaline IM for anaphylaxis: 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) of 1:1000 IM, repeated every 5 minutes as needed.

sections.heading: Observation and monitoring
items: Lower threshold for admission and antivenom in children.
Serial NMJ examination (ptosis, head lift, gag), 20WBCT, and circumferential limb measurement.
Pain management with age-appropriate analgesia; avoid NSAIDs if any coagulopathy.

sections.heading: Counselling
items: Address parental anxiety; explain the rationale for adult-dose antivenom in a small child.
Tetanus immunisation status, return advice for serum sickness, and follow-up wound care.

redFlags: Rapid swelling crossing a major joint within an hour — give antivenom.
Bite to face/neck — anticipate airway compromise.
Profound shock — aggressive resuscitation and early antivenom.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Prevention and Clinical Management of Snakebite in Africa (2010)

title: Snakebite in pregnancy
summary: Antivenom is NOT contraindicated in pregnancy — untreated systemic envenomation is far more dangerous to the mother and fetus than the small risk of antivenom reaction; standard adult dosing applies.

sections.heading: Key principles
items: Untreated systemic envenomation causes maternal shock, coagulopathy, neurotoxicity and fetal loss.
Antivenom (e.g. SAIMR polyvalent) is given at standard adult doses for the standard indications — pregnancy is NOT a contraindication.
Risk-benefit clearly favours treatment of any systemic envenomation.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: Standard maternal monitoring (BP, HR, RR, SpO2, urine output) plus fetal heart rate monitoring appropriate for gestation.
Watch for placental abruption (haemotoxic venom + coagulopathy + hypotension) — abdominal pain, PV bleeding, uterine tone changes.
20WBCT and NMJ assessment as usual.

sections.heading: Treatment notes
items: Adrenaline IM at standard adult dose for anaphylaxis during antivenom — withholding adrenaline for fear of fetal effects causes worse outcomes.
Tetanus immunisation is safe in pregnancy.
Multi-disciplinary involvement: obstetrics, toxicology, anaesthesia for any unstable case.

redFlags: Decreased fetal movements, PV bleeding, abdominal pain — assess for abruption.
Maternal shock or coagulopathy — antivenom is more urgent in pregnancy, not less.

title: Snake identification in the clinical setting
summary: Species identification helps refine prognosis and choice of antivenom but must NEVER delay clinical management — syndrome-based treatment is the WHO-recommended default and a missed identification does not harm a patient whose syndrome is treated.

sections.heading: Safe identification practice
items: If the snake has been killed already and can be safely transported in a sealed container, accept it for identification — but do NOT ask anyone to go back and find or kill the snake.
Do NOT bring a live snake into a clinical area — risk to staff and other patients.
A photograph (from a safe distance) is usually sufficient — instruct callers to photograph rather than capture.
Even a dead snake can deliver a reflex bite for up to an hour after death — handle with a long stick or tongs, head shielded.

sections.heading: Clinical clues to species
items: Marked local swelling + necrosis with no neurotoxicity → think viper (puff adder) or spitting cobra.
Minimal local swelling + descending paralysis → think mamba or non-spitting cobra.
Eye spray injury → spitting cobra (Naja nigricollis, N. pallida) or rinkhals.
Apparently mild bite followed by delayed bleeding (24–72 h) → suspect boomslang or twig snake.
Saw-scaled / rasping warning sound + bleeding diathesis → Echis sp.

sections.heading: Operational rule
items: Do NOT delay antivenom or 20WBCT waiting for species ID.
Treat by syndrome (cyto/neuro/haemo) using the available polyvalent antivenom; switch to monovalent (boomslang) if species/syndrome dictates.
Document any identification (photograph, expert opinion) in the clinical record; flag uncertain identifications.

redFlags: Misidentification of a venomous snake as harmless — assume venomous if any uncertainty in a patient with a bite mark.
Patient or family handling a captured live snake — secure the snake and decontaminate the area; treat any new bites.

title: Observation period and discharge criteria after snakebite
summary: All credible snakebite victims need a minimum 24-hour observation with serial examination and 20WBCT, extended to 48–72 hours for suspected boomslang/twig snake bites; discharge planning must include serum sickness counselling and return advice.

sections.heading: Minimum observation
items: Observe ALL credible snakebite victims for at least 24 hours with serial vital signs, limb examination, NMJ assessment and 20WBCT every 6 hours.
Extend to at least 48–72 hours if suspected boomslang or twig snake bite, because coagulopathy can present late.
For neurotoxic envenomation that received antivenom, continue close observation (often in HDU/ICU) until paralysis is clearly resolving.

sections.heading: Discharge criteria (all must be met)
items: Asymptomatic with stable, non-progressing local swelling for at least 12 hours.
Normal serial 20WBCT (most recent within 6 hours of discharge).
Normal vital signs, normal urine output and normal mental status.
If neurotoxic envenomation was treated: full resolution of bulbar weakness and adequate respiratory effort (single-breath count above 25, normal SpO2 on room air).
Tetanus prophylaxis given per status.

sections.heading: Discharge counselling
items: Wound care advice and follow-up appointment for cytotoxic bites and any necrotic wounds.
Warn about serum sickness 5–14 days after antivenom — urticaria, fever, joint pain — and to return.
Provide a written record of the species (if known), antivenom product/dose/batch, and any complications.
Snake-avoidance advice: footwear, torch at night, safe handling of woodpiles and grass.

redFlags: Persistent abnormal 20WBCT — do NOT discharge; repeat antivenom and reassess.
Any recurring bulbar weakness, ptosis or new bleeding — re-admit.
Discharge before 48–72 hours after a confirmed boomslang or twig snake bite — unsafe regardless of how well the patient appears.
